# Compatibility policy context

## Authority and reading map

This workspace records historical upstream policy, not a downstream implementation.
The evaluation cutoff is **2020-07-20**, the latest and only date in the
[evidence index](../evidence/index.txt). Do not interpret it as today's policy.
The index explicitly supplies no downstream adoption or feature-specific exception
approval evidence; no downstream runtime access is supplied either.

The authoritative local [PEP 387 snapshot](../evidence/compatibility-2020-07-20.rst)
is marked **Active**, **Process**, authored by Benjamin Peterson, with Brett
Cannon as BDFL-Delegate on behalf of the steering council. The index records its
upstream commit URL and SHA-256. Requirements below summarize that snapshot;
section names identify the source passages without duplicating the source.

- [Scope and rationale](#scope-and-rationale)
- [Deprecation and notices](#deprecation-and-notices)
- [Exceptions](#exceptions)
- [History and unresolved questions](#history-and-unresolved-questions)
- [Maintaining this context](#maintaining-this-context)

## Scope and rationale

Source: snapshot, “Rationale” and “Backwards Compatibility Rules.”

The policy protects existing third-party code relying on Python's core language
and standard library. Backwards incompatibility means preexisting code ceases to
comparatively function after a change; the definition is deliberately not precise.
Ask the Python development team and/or steering council for guidance when unsure.

Public API coverage includes:

- Reference-manual syntax and behavior, and the C API.
- Function, class, module, attribute, and method names and types.
- Return values, side effects, and raised exceptions for given arguments, while
  allowing reasonable bug fixes; argument and return-value positions and expected types.
- Subclass behavior, including when overridden methods are called.
- Documented exceptions and their triggering semantics, and exceptions commonly
  raised in EAFP usage (attempting an operation and handling failure).

Excluded items may change or disappear at any time: underscore-prefixed names
and types (except special names), anything publicly documented as private,
imported modules unless explicitly documented as public API, internal-class
inheritance patterns, and test suites. Explicitly **Provisional** modules/APIs
under PEP 411 are also outside these compatibility rules. Importing a module does
not by itself make it part of the importing module's public API.

Incompatibilities should offer a large benefit relative to breakage and be easy
to resolve in affected code. Adding a standard-library module that shadows a
third-party package is generally unacceptable; adding a method or attribute that
conflicts through inheritance is likely reasonable. These are qualified judgments,
not blanket permissions. Source: “Basic policy for backwards compatibility.”

## Deprecation and notices

Source: “Basic policy for backwards compatibility” and “Making Incompatible Changes.”

An API's behavior must not change incompatibly between consecutive releases
unless it goes through deprecation. A feature cannot be removed without notice
between consecutive releases. The basic policy explicitly requires a deprecation
period of **at least two years**, citing the yearly release process.

The prescribed sequence is:

1. Discuss the change in a suitable forum (bug tracker, python-dev, python-list,
   or relevant SIG); a PEP or similar document may be appropriate. Seek affected
   users' input.
2. Add a warning. For a behavior change, a new function or method may provide the
   new behavior and old usage should warn. For removal, warn whenever the API is
   entered. Usually use `DeprecationWarning`; `PendingDeprecationWarning` may be
   used in special cases where old and new APIs coexist for many releases.
   Compiler warnings are acceptable. The warning message should identify the
   expected release for the incompatibility to become default and link to an
   issue where users can give feedback.
3. Let the warning appear in **at least two major Python versions**; more than
   two releases is allowed.
4. Review feedback, including from users absent from the original discussion;
   reconsider if appropriate.
5. Once the declared version is reached and the process completed, make the
   behavior change/removal default or permanent and remove the old version and warning.

**Internal timing tension:** the basic policy measures the minimum in years,
while step 3 measures warning exposure in “major Python versions” and then refers
to “releases.” The snapshot does not define how these units align. Do not silently
replace either requirement with the other or infer a specific removal date from
a release count alone. A concrete schedule needs both requirements checked and
any unresolved interpretation clarified with upstream authority.

**Soft deprecation is not specified in this snapshot.** It supplies no definition,
warning semantics, removal commitment, or timing rule for that term. The special
case for `PendingDeprecationWarning` is explicit; it is not evidence of a separate
soft-deprecation policy.

## Exceptions

Source: “Basic policy for backwards compatibility.”

The **steering council** may grant exceptions, including shortening the required
deprecation period. Exceptions are only for extreme situations such as dangerously
broken or insecure features, or features no one could reasonably depend on
(for example, completely obsolete platforms). Those examples do not automatically
authorize an exception. The delegate metadata does not establish independent
feature-specific approval. No such approval is supplied in this packet.

## History and unresolved questions

Source: snapshot header and [evidence index](../evidence/index.txt).

The header records creation on **2009-06-18** and post-history dates
**2009-06-19** and **2020-06-12**. Those dates establish historical milestones,
not the text or effects of earlier decisions. `Version` and `Last-Modified` are
unexpanded placeholders. Use the index's **2020-07-20** snapshot date as the
evidence cutoff, not as an inferred policy adoption date.

Only one revision is supplied, so no earlier rule, policy transition, or
supersession can be verified. In particular, do not invent an earlier timing
minimum or import later Python policy. The timing tension above remains unresolved.
Other unknowns are downstream adoption/enforcement, any feature's public or
provisional classification, warning start and target releases, feedback, and
exception approvals. The snapshot references PEPs 411 and 602, but their full
texts are not supplied; only the statements here about them are supported locally.

## Maintaining this context

Keep raw evidence unchanged. When new authorized evidence arrives, update the
cutoff and operative summary with local citations. Preserve significant prior
decisions, rationale, exceptions, and unresolved issues; explicitly state which
rule a new decision supersedes and when, rather than leaving conflicting old
instructions operative. Keep upstream policy separate from proven downstream
adoption and feature-specific approvals. Retain unique useful details without
copying whole sources or accumulating session diaries.

PEP: 387
Title: Backwards Compatibility Policy
Version: $Revision$
Last-Modified: $Date$
Author: Benjamin Peterson <benjamin@python.org>
BDFL-Delegate: Brett Cannon (on behalf of the steering council)
Discussions-To: https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-387-backwards-compatibilty-policy/
Status: Active
Type: Process
Content-Type: text/x-rst
Created: 18-Jun-2009
Post-History: 19-Jun-2009, 12-Jun-2020


Abstract
========

This PEP outlines Python's backwards compatibility policy.


Rationale
=========

As one of the most used programming languages today [#tiobe]_, the
Python core language and its standard library play a critical role in
millions of applications and libraries. This is fantastic. However, it
means the development team must be very careful not to break this
existing 3rd party code with new releases.

This PEP takes the perspective that "backwards incompatibility" means
preexisting code ceases to comparatively function after a change. It is
acknowledged that this is not a concrete definition, but the expectation
is people in general understand what is meant by
"backwards incompatibility", and if they are unsure they may ask the
Python development team and/or steering council for guidance.


Backwards Compatibility Rules
=============================

This policy applies to all public APIs.  These include:

- Syntax and behavior of these constructs as defined by the reference
  manual.

- The C-API.

- Function, class, module, attribute, and method names and types.

- Given a set of arguments, the return value, side effects, and raised
  exceptions of a function.  This does not preclude changes from
  reasonable bug fixes.

- The position and expected types of arguments and returned values.

- Behavior of classes with regards to subclasses: the conditions under
  which overridden methods are called.

- Documented exceptions and the semantics which lead to their raising.

- Exceptions commonly raised in EAFP scenarios.

Others are explicitly not part of the public API.  They can change or
be removed at any time in any way.  These include:

- Function, class, module, attribute, method, and C-API names and
  types that are prefixed by "_" (except special names).

- Anything documented publicly as being private.

- Imported modules (unless explicitly documented as part of the public
  API; e.g. importing the ``bacon`` module in the ``spam`` does not
  automatically mean ``spam.bacon`` is part of the public API unless
  it is documented as such).

- Inheritance patterns of internal classes.

- Test suites.  (Anything in the ``Lib/test`` directory or test
  subdirectories of packages.)

- Backward compatibility rules do not apply to any module or API that is
  explicitly documented as **Provisional** per PEP 411.


Basic policy for backwards compatibility
----------------------------------------

* In general, incompatibilities should have a large benefit to
  breakage ratio, and the incompatibility should be easy to resolve in
  affected code.  For example, adding an stdlib module with the same
  name as a third party package is generally not acceptable.  Adding
  a method or attribute that conflicts with 3rd party code through
  inheritance, however, is likely reasonable.

* Unless it is going through the deprecation process below, the
  behavior of an API *must* not change in an incompatible fashion
  between any two consecutive releases.  Python's yearly release
  process (:pep:`602`) means that the deprecation period must last at
  least two years.

* Similarly a feature cannot be removed without notice between any two
  consecutive releases.

* The steering council may grant exceptions to this policy. In
  particular, they may shorten the required deprecation period for a
  feature. Exceptions are only granted for extreme situations such as
  dangerously broken or insecure features or features no one could
  reasonably be depending on (e.g., support for completely obsolete
  platforms).


Making Incompatible Changes
===========================

Making an incompatible change is a gradual process performed over
several releases:

1. Discuss the change.  Depending on the degree of incompatibility,
   this could be on the bug tracker, python-dev, python-list, or the
   appropriate SIG.  A PEP or similar document may be written.
   Hopefully users of the affected API will pipe up to comment.

2. Add a warning.  If behavior is changing, the API may gain a new
   function or method to perform the new behavior; old usage should
   raise the warning.  If an API is being removed, simply warn
   whenever it is entered.  ``DeprecationWarning`` is the usual
   warning category to use, but ``PendingDeprecationWarning`` may be
   used in special cases where the old and new versions of the API will
   coexist for many releases [#warnings]_. Compiler warnings are also
   acceptable. The warning message should include the release the
   incompatibility is expected to become the default and a link to an
   issue that users can post feedback to.

3. Wait for the warning to appear in at least two major Python
   versions. It's fine to wait more than two releases.

4. See if there's any feedback.  Users not involved in the original
   discussions may comment now after seeing the warning.  Perhaps
   reconsider.

5. The behavior change or feature removal may now be made default or
   permanent having reached the declared version. Remove the old
   version and warning.


References
==========

.. [#tiobe] TIOBE Programming Community Index

   http://www.tiobe.com/index.php/content/paperinfo/tpci/index.html

.. [#warnings] The warnings module

   http://docs.python.org/library/warnings.html


Copyright
=========

This document has been placed in the public domain.

# Compatibility policy context

## Authority and reading map

This workspace records historical upstream policy, not a downstream implementation.
The evaluation cutoff is **2023-07-03**, the latest supplied date in the
[evidence index](../evidence/index.txt). Do not interpret it as today's policy.
The index explicitly supplies no downstream adoption or feature-specific exception
approval evidence; no downstream runtime access is supplied either.

The authoritative local [PEP 387 snapshot](../evidence/compatibility-2023-07-03.rst)
is marked **Active**, **Process**, authored by Benjamin Peterson, with Brett
Cannon as PEP-Delegate. The index records its
upstream commit URL and SHA-256. Requirements below summarize that snapshot;
section names identify the source passages without duplicating the source.

- [Scope and rationale](#scope-and-rationale)
- [Deprecation and notices](#deprecation-and-notices)
- [Soft deprecation](#soft-deprecation)
- [Exceptions](#exceptions)
- [History and unresolved questions](#history-and-unresolved-questions)
- [Maintaining this context](#maintaining-this-context)

## Scope and rationale

Source: [2023 snapshot](../evidence/compatibility-2023-07-03.rst), “Rationale” and “Backwards Compatibility Rules.”

The policy protects existing third-party code relying on Python's core language
and standard library. Backwards incompatibility means preexisting code ceases to
comparatively function after a change; the definition is deliberately not precise.
Ask the Python development team and/or steering council for guidance when unsure.

Public API coverage includes:

- Reference-manual syntax and behavior, and the C API.
- Function, class, module, attribute, and method names and types.
- Return values, side effects, and raised exceptions for given arguments, while
  allowing reasonable bug fixes; argument and return-value positions and expected types.
- Subclass behavior, including when overridden methods are called.
- Documented exceptions and their triggering semantics, and exceptions commonly
  raised in EAFP usage (attempting an operation and handling failure).

Excluded items may change or disappear at any time: underscore-prefixed names
and types (except special names), anything publicly documented as private,
imported modules unless explicitly documented as public API, internal-class
inheritance patterns, and test suites. Explicitly **Provisional** modules/APIs
under PEP 411 are also outside these compatibility rules. Importing a module does
not by itself make it part of the importing module's public API. An undocumented
item is **not automatically private**; lack of documentation alone is no exemption.

Incompatibilities should offer a large benefit relative to breakage and be easy
to resolve in affected code. Adding a standard-library module that shadows a
third-party package is generally unacceptable; adding a method or attribute that
conflicts through inheritance is likely reasonable. These are qualified judgments,
not blanket permissions. Source: [2023 snapshot](../evidence/compatibility-2023-07-03.rst),
“Basic policy for backwards compatibility.”

## Deprecation and notices

Source: [2023 snapshot](../evidence/compatibility-2023-07-03.rst),
“Basic policy for backwards compatibility” and “Making Incompatible Changes.”

An API's behavior must not change incompatibly between consecutive releases
unless it goes through deprecation. A feature cannot be removed without notice
between consecutive releases. The basic policy explicitly requires a deprecation
period of **at least two years**, citing the yearly release process.

The prescribed sequence is:

1. Discuss the change in a suitable forum (bug tracker, python-dev, python-list,
   or relevant SIG); a PEP or similar document may be appropriate. Seek affected
   users' input.
2. Add a warning to the current `main` branch. For a behavior change, a new
   function or method may provide the new behavior and old usage should warn. For removal, warn whenever the API is
   entered. Usually use `DeprecationWarning`; `PendingDeprecationWarning` may be
   used in special cases where old and new APIs coexist for many releases.
   For the C API, a compiler warning generated by `Py_DEPRECATED` is acceptable.
   The warning message should identify the expected release for the incompatibility to become default and link to an
   issue where users can give feedback.
3. Let the warning appear in **at least two minor Python versions of the same
   major version, or one minor version in an older major version**. The source
   example permits a warning in 3.10.0 to lead to a change no earlier than 3.12
   or 4.0, subject to the timing tension below. Longer waits are allowed:
   deprecated behavior with little maintenance overhead and security risk may
   remain indefinitely (or until circumstances change). When a new feature
   replaces an old one, removal should generally wait until the last Python
   version **without** the replacement reaches end of support.
4. Review feedback, including from users absent from the original discussion;
   reconsider if appropriate.
5. Once the declared version is reached and the process completed, the behavior
   change/removal may be made default or permanent; remove the old version and warning.
6. If users cannot be provided a warning, consult the steering council. The
   basic policy also requires consultation for changes unable to raise a
   deprecation warning.

**Internal timing tension:** the basic policy still mandates at least two years,
while step 3 allows one minor version in an older major version before a major
version transition. The source does not explain how that alternative satisfies
the two-year minimum if the transition occurs sooner. Do not treat it as an
implicit exception or infer an actual removal date from version numbers alone.
Check both requirements and seek upstream clarification for an unresolved schedule.

## Soft deprecation

Source: [2023 snapshot](../evidence/compatibility-2023-07-03.rst), “Soft Deprecation.”

A soft-deprecated API should not be used in new code but remains safe for existing
code. It stays documented and tested, with no further enhancements. Soft
deprecation does **not** imply scheduling removal and issues **no warning**;
it is mentioned only in documentation. That documentation should explain why to
avoid the API and propose a replacement if possible.

A later regular (“hard”) deprecation must follow the full backwards compatibility
rules; prior soft deprecation grants no exception. Do not credit time spent soft
deprecated as warning exposure or confuse it with `PendingDeprecationWarning`,
which remains a special case in the regular warning process.

## Exceptions

Source: [2023 snapshot](../evidence/compatibility-2023-07-03.rst),
“Basic policy for backwards compatibility.”

The **steering council** may grant exceptions, including shortening the required
deprecation period. Exceptions are only for extreme situations such as dangerously
broken or insecure features, or features no one could reasonably depend on
(for example, completely obsolete platforms). Those examples do not automatically
authorize an exception. The delegate metadata does not establish independent
feature-specific approval. No such approval is supplied in this packet.

## History and unresolved questions

Sources: [evidence index](../evidence/index.txt),
[2020 snapshot](../evidence/compatibility-2020-07-20.rst), and
[2023 snapshot](../evidence/compatibility-2023-07-03.rst). The 2023 snapshot governs
this summary; the following earlier wording is historical, not an alternate rule.

| Topic | Earlier evidence (2020-07-20) | Current evidence (2023-07-03) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Timing | Two-year minimum, but step 3 said “at least two major Python versions,” then “releases,” leaving the units unclear. | Two-year minimum retained; step 3 supersedes the old wording with minor-version exposure and the major-transition alternative above. The earlier ambiguity is replaced by the remaining timing tension. |
| Warnings | Add a warning; compiler warnings broadly accepted. | Specifies current `main` and C API `Py_DEPRECATED`; explicitly requires council consultation when warnings cannot be provided. |
| Longer retention | More than two releases allowed. | Adds indefinite retention for low overhead/risk and waiting for end of support of versions without the replacement. |
| Soft deprecation | No definition, warning semantics, removal commitment, or timing rule supplied. | Adds the documentation-only status and full regular-deprecation requirements for any later transition. The earlier absence is no longer the current evidence limit. |
| Private scope | Publicly documented private items excluded. | Clarifies that undocumented items are not automatically private; other scope rules remain. |
| Authority | Active Process PEP; Benjamin Peterson, BDFL-Delegate Brett Cannon on behalf of the steering council. | Active Process PEP; same author, PEP-Delegate Brett Cannon. Council exception authority and extreme-situation criteria remain. |

Both headers record creation on **2009-06-18** and post-history dates
**2009-06-19** and **2020-06-12**; the newer header adds **2023-06-16**.
These establish milestones, not exact adoption dates for individual changes.
`Version` and `Last-Modified` remain unexpanded placeholders. The index provides
upstream commit URLs and SHA-256 values for both snapshots; its latest date is
the evidence cutoff, not an inferred adoption date. No intervening revisions are
supplied, so the exact timing of each change between snapshots is unknown.

Other unknowns are downstream adoption/enforcement, any feature's public or
provisional classification, warning start and target releases, feedback,
end-of-support schedules, and exception approvals. No downstream runtime access
is supplied. The snapshots reference PEPs 411 and 602, but their full texts are
not supplied; only the statements here about them are supported locally. Do not
import later Python policy or treat missing feature-specific evidence as approval.

## Maintaining this context

Keep raw evidence unchanged. When new authorized evidence arrives, update the
cutoff and operative summary with local citations. Preserve significant prior
decisions, rationale, exceptions, and unresolved issues; explicitly state which
rule a new decision supersedes and when, rather than leaving conflicting old
instructions operative. Keep upstream policy separate from proven downstream

“Basic policy for backwards compatibility.”

between consecutive releases. The basic policy explicitly requires a deprecation
period of **at least two years**, citing the yearly release process.

   issue where users can give feedback.

   version **without** the replacement reaches end of support.

PEP: 387
Title: Backwards Compatibility Policy
Version: $Revision$
Last-Modified: $Date$
Author: Benjamin Peterson <benjamin@python.org>
BDFL-Delegate: Brett Cannon (on behalf of the steering council)
Discussions-To: https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-387-backwards-compatibilty-policy/
Status: Active
Type: Process
Content-Type: text/x-rst
Created: 18-Jun-2009
Post-History: 19-Jun-2009, 12-Jun-2020


Abstract
========

This PEP outlines Python's backwards compatibility policy.


Rationale
=========

As one of the most used programming languages today [#tiobe]_, the
Python core language and its standard library play a critical role in
millions of applications and libraries. This is fantastic. However, it
means the development team must be very careful not to break this
existing 3rd party code with new releases.

This PEP takes the perspective that "backwards incompatibility" means
preexisting code ceases to comparatively function after a change. It is
acknowledged that this is not a concrete definition, but the expectation
is people in general understand what is meant by
"backwards incompatibility", and if they are unsure they may ask the
Python development team and/or steering council for guidance.


Backwards Compatibility Rules
=============================

This policy applies to all public APIs.  These include:

- Syntax and behavior of these constructs as defined by the reference
  manual.

- The C-API.

- Function, class, module, attribute, and method names and types.

- Given a set of arguments, the return value, side effects, and raised
  exceptions of a function.  This does not preclude changes from
  reasonable bug fixes.

- The position and expected types of arguments and returned values.

- Behavior of classes with regards to subclasses: the conditions under
  which overridden methods are called.

- Documented exceptions and the semantics which lead to their raising.

- Exceptions commonly raised in EAFP scenarios.

Others are explicitly not part of the public API.  They can change or
be removed at any time in any way.  These include:

- Function, class, module, attribute, method, and C-API names and
  types that are prefixed by "_" (except special names).

- Anything documented publicly as being private.

- Imported modules (unless explicitly documented as part of the public
  API; e.g. importing the ``bacon`` module in the ``spam`` does not
  automatically mean ``spam.bacon`` is part of the public API unless
  it is documented as such).

- Inheritance patterns of internal classes.

- Test suites.  (Anything in the ``Lib/test`` directory or test
  subdirectories of packages.)

- Backward compatibility rules do not apply to any module or API that is
  explicitly documented as **Provisional** per PEP 411.


Basic policy for backwards compatibility
----------------------------------------

* In general, incompatibilities should have a large benefit to
  breakage ratio, and the incompatibility should be easy to resolve in
  affected code.  For example, adding an stdlib module with the same
  name as a third party package is generally not acceptable.  Adding
  a method or attribute that conflicts with 3rd party code through
  inheritance, however, is likely reasonable.

* Unless it is going through the deprecation process below, the
  behavior of an API *must* not change in an incompatible fashion
  between any two consecutive releases.  Python's yearly release
  process (:pep:`602`) means that the deprecation period must last at
  least two years.

* Similarly a feature cannot be removed without notice between any two
  consecutive releases.

* The steering council may grant exceptions to this policy. In
  particular, they may shorten the required deprecation period for a
  feature. Exceptions are only granted for extreme situations such as
  dangerously broken or insecure features or features no one could
  reasonably be depending on (e.g., support for completely obsolete
  platforms).


Making Incompatible Changes
===========================

Making an incompatible change is a gradual process performed over
several releases:

1. Discuss the change.  Depending on the degree of incompatibility,
   this could be on the bug tracker, python-dev, python-list, or the
   appropriate SIG.  A PEP or similar document may be written.
   Hopefully users of the affected API will pipe up to comment.

2. Add a warning.  If behavior is changing, the API may gain a new
   function or method to perform the new behavior; old usage should
   raise the warning.  If an API is being removed, simply warn
   whenever it is entered.  ``DeprecationWarning`` is the usual
   warning category to use, but ``PendingDeprecationWarning`` may be
   used in special cases where the old and new versions of the API will
   coexist for many releases [#warnings]_. Compiler warnings are also
   acceptable. The warning message should include the release the
   incompatibility is expected to become the default and a link to an
   issue that users can post feedback to.

3. Wait for the warning to appear in at least two major Python
   versions. It's fine to wait more than two releases.

4. See if there's any feedback.  Users not involved in the original
   discussions may comment now after seeing the warning.  Perhaps
   reconsider.

5. The behavior change or feature removal may now be made default or
   permanent having reached the declared version. Remove the old
   version and warning.


References
==========

.. [#tiobe] TIOBE Programming Community Index

   http://www.tiobe.com/index.php/content/paperinfo/tpci/index.html

.. [#warnings] The warnings module

   http://docs.python.org/library/warnings.html

=========

  automatically considered private.

  dangerously broken or insecure features or features no one could
  reasonably be depending on (e.g., support for completely obsolete

   major version (e.g. for a warning in Python 3.10.0, you either wait

# Compatibility policy context

## Authority and reading map

This workspace records historical upstream policy, not a downstream implementation.
The evaluation cutoff is **2025-02-24**, the latest supplied date in the
[evidence index](../evidence/index.txt). Do not interpret it as today's policy.
The index explicitly supplies no downstream adoption or feature-specific exception
approval evidence; no downstream runtime access is supplied either.

The authoritative local [PEP 387 snapshot](../evidence/compatibility-2025-02-24.rst)
is marked **Active**, **Process**, authored by Benjamin Peterson, with Brett
Cannon as PEP-Delegate. The index records its
upstream commit URL and SHA-256. Requirements below summarize that snapshot;
section names identify the source passages without duplicating the source.

- [Scope and rationale](#scope-and-rationale)
- [Deprecation and notices](#deprecation-and-notices)
- [Soft deprecation](#soft-deprecation)
- [Exceptions](#exceptions)
- [History and unresolved questions](#history-and-unresolved-questions)
- [Maintaining this context](#maintaining-this-context)

## Scope and rationale

Source: [2025 snapshot](../evidence/compatibility-2025-02-24.rst), “Rationale” and “Backwards Compatibility Rules.”

The policy protects existing third-party code relying on Python's core language
and standard library. Backwards incompatibility means preexisting code ceases to
comparatively function after a change; the definition is deliberately not precise.
Ask the Python development team and/or steering council for guidance when unsure.

Public API coverage includes:

- Reference-manual syntax and behavior, and the C API.
- Function, class, module, attribute, and method names and types.
- Return values, side effects, and raised exceptions for given arguments, while
  allowing reasonable bug fixes; argument and return-value positions and expected types.
- Subclass behavior, including when overridden methods are called.
- Documented exceptions and their triggering semantics, and exceptions commonly
  raised in EAFP usage (attempting an operation and handling failure).

Excluded items may change or disappear at any time: underscore-prefixed names
and types (except special names), anything publicly documented as private,
imported modules unless explicitly documented as public API, internal-class
inheritance patterns, and test suites. Explicitly **Provisional** modules/APIs
under PEP 411 are also outside these compatibility rules. Importing a module does
not by itself make it part of the importing module's public API. An undocumented
item is **not automatically private**; lack of documentation alone is no exemption.

Incompatibilities should offer a large benefit relative to breakage and be easy
to resolve in affected code. Adding a standard-library module that shadows a
third-party package is generally unacceptable; adding a method or attribute that
conflicts through inheritance is likely reasonable. These are qualified judgments,
not blanket permissions. Source: [2025 snapshot](../evidence/compatibility-2025-02-24.rst),
“Basic policy for backwards compatibility.”

## Deprecation and notices

Source: [2025 snapshot](../evidence/compatibility-2025-02-24.rst),
“Basic policy for backwards compatibility” and “Making Incompatible Changes.”

An API's behavior must not change incompatibly between consecutive releases
unless it goes through deprecation. A feature cannot be removed without notice
between consecutive releases. The basic policy explicitly requires a deprecation
period of **at least two years**, citing the yearly release process. Step 3 now
**prefers five years before removal** (warning in 3.10, removal in 3.15), matching
the stated current lifetime of a minor release. This is a preference, not a new
mandatory minimum; it does not replace the notice or warning-exposure rules.

The prescribed sequence is:

1. Discuss the change in a suitable forum (bug tracker, python-dev, python-list,
   or relevant SIG); a PEP or similar document may be appropriate. Seek affected
   users' input.
2. Add a warning to the current `main` branch. For a behavior change, a new
   function or method may provide the new behavior and old usage should warn. For removal, warn whenever the API is
   entered. Usually use `DeprecationWarning`; `PendingDeprecationWarning` may be
   used in special cases where old and new APIs coexist for many releases.
   For the C API, a compiler warning generated by `Py_DEPRECATED` is acceptable.
   The warning message should identify the expected release for the incompatibility to become default and link to an
   issue where users can give feedback. When feasible, also add `@deprecated`
   in typeshed (PEP 702) so static type-checker users receive another notice;
   this supplements the warning process.
3. Let the warning appear in **at least two minor Python versions of the same
   major version, or one minor version in an older major version**. The source
   example permits a warning in 3.10.0 to lead to a change no earlier than 3.12
   or 4.0, subject to the timing tension below and the five-year removal preference.
   Longer retention remains allowed:
   deprecated behavior with little maintenance overhead and security risk may
   remain indefinitely (or until circumstances change). When a new feature
   replaces an old one, removal should generally wait until the last Python
   version **without** the replacement reaches end of support.
4. Review feedback, including from users absent from the original discussion;
   reconsider if appropriate.
5. Once the declared version is reached and the process completed, the behavior
   change/removal may be made default or permanent; remove the old version and warning.
6. If users cannot be provided a warning, consult the steering council. The
   basic policy also requires consultation for changes unable to raise a
   deprecation warning.

**Internal timing tension:** the basic policy still mandates at least two years,
while step 3 allows one minor version in an older major version before a major
version transition. The source does not explain how that alternative satisfies
the two-year minimum if the transition occurs sooner. Do not treat it as an
implicit exception or infer an actual removal date from version numbers alone.
Check both requirements and seek upstream clarification for an unresolved schedule.

## Soft deprecation

Source: [2025 snapshot](../evidence/compatibility-2025-02-24.rst), “Soft Deprecation.”

A soft-deprecated API should not be used in new code but remains safe for existing
code. It stays documented and tested, with no further enhancements. Soft
deprecation does **not** imply scheduling removal and issues **no warning**;
it is mentioned only in documentation. That documentation should explain why to
avoid the API and propose a replacement if possible.

A later regular (“hard”) deprecation must follow the full backwards compatibility
rules; prior soft deprecation grants no exception. Do not credit time spent soft
deprecated as warning exposure or confuse it with `PendingDeprecationWarning`,
which remains a special case in the regular warning process.

## Exceptions

Source: [2025 snapshot](../evidence/compatibility-2025-02-24.rst),
“Basic policy for backwards compatibility.”

The **steering council** may grant exceptions, including shortening the required
deprecation period. Exceptions are only for extreme situations such as dangerously
broken or insecure features, or features no one could reasonably depend on
(for example, completely obsolete platforms). Those examples do not automatically
authorize an exception. The delegate metadata does not establish independent
feature-specific approval. No such approval is supplied in this packet.

## History and unresolved questions

Sources: [evidence index](../evidence/index.txt),
[2020 snapshot](../evidence/compatibility-2020-07-20.rst),
[2023 snapshot](../evidence/compatibility-2023-07-03.rst), and
[2025 snapshot](../evidence/compatibility-2025-02-24.rst), including its “Changelog.”
The **2025 snapshot supersedes the 2023 snapshot as this summary's authority**.
Earlier wording below is historical, not an alternate operative rule.

| Topic | Earlier decision and supersession | Position at the 2025 cutoff |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Timing | 2020 required two years but step 3 said “two major Python versions,” then “releases,” leaving units unclear. The 2023 snapshot replaced that wording with minor-version exposure and a major-transition alternative. | Retains the two-year minimum and 2023 exposure rules; adds a preferred five-year wait before removal. The major-transition timing tension remains unresolved. |
| Warnings | 2020 broadly accepted compiler warnings. By 2023, the procedure specified current `main`, C API `Py_DEPRECATED`, and council consultation when warnings cannot be provided. | Retains those rules; adds typeshed `@deprecated` when feasible as an additional static notice. |
| Longer retention | 2020 allowed more than two releases. By 2023, low overhead/risk could justify indefinite retention, and replacement guidance generally waited for end of support of versions without it. | Retains both safeguards alongside the five-year preference; five years is not an automatic removal deadline. |
| Soft deprecation | 2020 supplied no definition or timing semantics. The 2023 snapshot added documentation-only status, no scheduled removal or warning, and full regular-deprecation rules for any later transition. | Unchanged; the earlier absence is no longer an evidence limit. |
| Private scope | 2020 excluded publicly documented private items. By 2023, the text clarified that undocumented items are not automatically private. | Clarification and other scope rules retained. |
| Authority | 2020: Active Process PEP; Benjamin Peterson, BDFL-Delegate Brett Cannon on behalf of the steering council. By 2023: same status and author, PEP-Delegate Brett Cannon. | Same as 2023; council exception authority and extreme-situation criteria retained. Header now records “Replaces: 291.” |

The latest source's changelog supplies dates absent from the earlier context:

- **2020-07-20:** initial accepted version.
- **2021-04-16:** clarification of warning duration.
- **2022-04-04:** explicit steering council consultation notes for exceptional cases.
- **2023-06-26:** multiple smaller updates and clarifications; the changelog does
  not separately date each wording change.
- **2023-07-03:** soft-deprecation section added.
- **2023-11-14:** `@deprecated` notice added per PEP 702.
- **2025-01-27:** five-year deprecation preference added.

All three headers record creation on **2009-06-18** and post-history dates
**2009-06-19** and **2020-06-12**. The 2023 header adds **2023-06-16**; the 2025
header also lists **2022-12-19**. Post-history entries are discussion milestones,
not exact adoption dates. `Version` and `Last-Modified` were unexpanded
placeholders in 2020 and 2023; they are absent in 2025. The index provides upstream
commit URLs and SHA-256 values for all three snapshots. Its latest date is the
evidence cutoff, not an inferred adoption date. No intervening snapshots are
supplied; use the latest changelog for the dates it explicitly records, without
inferring dates for other individual edits.

Other unknowns are downstream adoption/enforcement, any feature's public or
provisional classification, warning start and target releases, feedback,
end-of-support schedules, and exception approvals. No downstream runtime access
is supplied. The snapshots reference PEPs 411, 602, and 702, and the latest header names
PEP 291 as replaced, but those full texts are not supplied. Only the statements
here about them are supported locally. Do not
import later Python policy or treat missing feature-specific evidence as approval.

## Maintaining this context

Keep raw evidence unchanged. When new authorized evidence arrives, update the
cutoff and operative summary with local citations. Preserve significant prior
decisions, rationale, exceptions, and unresolved issues; explicitly state which
rule a new decision supersedes and when, rather than leaving conflicting old
instructions operative. Keep upstream policy separate from proven downstream
adoption and feature-specific approvals. Retain unique useful details without
copying whole sources or accumulating session diaries.

Title: Backwards Compatibility Policy

Last-Modified: $Date$
Author: Benjamin Peterson <benjamin@python.org>

Status: Active
Type: Process
Content-Type: text/x-rst

Abstract
========

This PEP outlines Python's backwards compatibility policy.


Rationale
=========

As one of the most used programming languages today [#tiobe]_, the
Python core language and its standard library play a critical role in
millions of applications and libraries. This is fantastic. However, it
means the development team must be very careful not to break this
existing 3rd party code with new releases.

This PEP takes the perspective that "backwards incompatibility" means
preexisting code ceases to comparatively function after a change. It is
acknowledged that this is not a concrete definition, but the expectation
is people in general understand what is meant by
"backwards incompatibility", and if they are unsure they may ask the
Python development team and/or steering council for guidance.


Backwards Compatibility Rules
=============================

This policy applies to all public APIs.  These include:

- Syntax and behavior of these constructs as defined by the reference
  manual.

- The C-API.

- Function, class, module, attribute, and method names and types.

- Given a set of arguments, the return value, side effects, and raised
  exceptions of a function.  This does not preclude changes from
  reasonable bug fixes.

- The position and expected types of arguments and returned values.

- Behavior of classes with regards to subclasses: the conditions under
  which overridden methods are called.

- Documented exceptions and the semantics which lead to their raising.

- Exceptions commonly raised in EAFP scenarios.

Others are explicitly not part of the public API.  They can change or
be removed at any time in any way.  These include:

- Function, class, module, attribute, method, and C-API names and
  types that are prefixed by "_" (except special names).

- Anything documented publicly as being private.

- Imported modules (unless explicitly documented as part of the public
  API; e.g. importing the ``bacon`` module in the ``spam`` does not
  automatically mean ``spam.bacon`` is part of the public API unless
  it is documented as such).

- Inheritance patterns of internal classes.

- Test suites.  (Anything in the ``Lib/test`` directory or test
  subdirectories of packages.)

- Backward compatibility rules do not apply to any module or API that is
  explicitly documented as **Provisional** per PEP 411.


Basic policy for backwards compatibility
----------------------------------------

* In general, incompatibilities should have a large benefit to
  breakage ratio, and the incompatibility should be easy to resolve in
  affected code.  For example, adding an stdlib module with the same
  name as a third party package is generally not acceptable.  Adding
  a method or attribute that conflicts with 3rd party code through
  inheritance, however, is likely reasonable.

* Unless it is going through the deprecation process below, the
  behavior of an API *must* not change in an incompatible fashion
  between any two consecutive releases.  Python's yearly release
  process (:pep:`602`) means that the deprecation period must last at
  least two years.

* Similarly a feature cannot be removed without notice between any two
  consecutive releases.

* The steering council may grant exceptions to this policy. In
  particular, they may shorten the required deprecation period for a
  feature. Exceptions are only granted for extreme situations such as
  dangerously broken or insecure features or features no one could
  reasonably be depending on (e.g., support for completely obsolete
  platforms).


Making Incompatible Changes
===========================

Making an incompatible change is a gradual process performed over
several releases:

1. Discuss the change.  Depending on the degree of incompatibility,
   this could be on the bug tracker, python-dev, python-list, or the
   appropriate SIG.  A PEP or similar document may be written.
   Hopefully users of the affected API will pipe up to comment.

2. Add a warning.  If behavior is changing, the API may gain a new
   function or method to perform the new behavior; old usage should
   raise the warning.  If an API is being removed, simply warn
   whenever it is entered.  ``DeprecationWarning`` is the usual
   warning category to use, but ``PendingDeprecationWarning`` may be
   used in special cases where the old and new versions of the API will
   coexist for many releases [#warnings]_. Compiler warnings are also
   acceptable. The warning message should include the release the
   incompatibility is expected to become the default and a link to an
   issue that users can post feedback to.

3. Wait for the warning to appear in at least two major Python
   versions. It's fine to wait more than two releases.

4. See if there's any feedback.  Users not involved in the original
   discussions may comment now after seeing the warning.  Perhaps
   reconsider.

5. The behavior change or feature removal may now be made default or
   permanent having reached the declared version. Remove the old
   version and warning.

   http://docs.python.org/library/warnings.html

# Compatibility policy context

## Authority and reading map

This workspace records historical upstream policy, not a downstream implementation.
The evaluation cutoff is **2025-02-24**, the latest supplied date in the
[evidence index](../evidence/index.txt). Do not interpret it as today's policy.
The index explicitly supplies no downstream adoption or feature-specific exception
approval evidence; no downstream runtime access is supplied either.

The authoritative local [PEP 387 snapshot](../evidence/compatibility-2025-02-24.rst)
is marked **Active**, **Process**, authored by Benjamin Peterson, with Brett
Cannon as PEP-Delegate. The index records its
upstream commit URL and SHA-256. Requirements below summarize that snapshot;
section names identify the source passages without duplicating the source.

- [Scope and rationale](#scope-and-rationale)
- [Deprecation and notices](#deprecation-and-notices)
- [Soft deprecation](#soft-deprecation)
- [Exceptions](#exceptions)
- [History and unresolved questions](#history-and-unresolved-questions)
- [Maintaining this context](#maintaining-this-context)

## Scope and rationale

Source: [2025 snapshot](../evidence/compatibility-2025-02-24.rst), “Rationale” and “Backwards Compatibility Rules.”

The policy protects existing third-party code relying on Python's core language
and standard library. Backwards incompatibility means preexisting code ceases to
comparatively function after a change; the definition is deliberately not precise.
Ask the Python development team and/or steering council for guidance when unsure.

Public API coverage includes:

- Reference-manual syntax and behavior, and the C API.
- Function, class, module, attribute, and method names and types.
- Return values, side effects, and raised exceptions for given arguments, while
  allowing reasonable bug fixes; argument and return-value positions and expected types.
- Subclass behavior, including when overridden methods are called.
- Documented exceptions and their triggering semantics, and exceptions commonly
  raised in EAFP usage (attempting an operation and handling failure).

Excluded items may change or disappear at any time: underscore-prefixed names
and types (except special names), anything publicly documented as private,
imported modules unless explicitly documented as public API, internal-class
inheritance patterns, and test suites. Explicitly **Provisional** modules/APIs
under PEP 411 are also outside these compatibility rules. Importing a module does
not by itself make it part of the importing module's public API. An undocumented
item is **not automatically private**; lack of documentation alone is no exemption.

Incompatibilities should offer a large benefit relative to breakage and be easy
to resolve in affected code. Adding a standard-library module that shadows a
third-party package is generally unacceptable; adding a method or attribute that
conflicts through inheritance is likely reasonable. These are qualified judgments,
not blanket permissions. Source: [2025 snapshot](../evidence/compatibility-2025-02-24.rst),
“Basic policy for backwards compatibility.”

## Deprecation and notices

Source: [2025 snapshot](../evidence/compatibility-2025-02-24.rst),
“Basic policy for backwards compatibility” and “Making Incompatible Changes.”

An API's behavior must not change incompatibly between consecutive releases
unless it goes through deprecation. A feature cannot be removed without notice
between consecutive releases. The basic policy explicitly requires a deprecation
period of **at least two years**, citing the yearly release process. Step 3 now
**prefers five years before removal** (warning in 3.10, removal in 3.15), matching
the stated current lifetime of a minor release. This is a preference, not a new
mandatory minimum; it does not replace the notice or warning-exposure rules.

The prescribed sequence is:

1. Discuss the change in a suitable forum (bug tracker, python-dev, python-list,
   or relevant SIG); a PEP or similar document may be appropriate. Seek affected
   users' input.

Discussions-To: https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-387-backwards-compatibilty-policy/
Status: Active
Type: Process
Content-Type: text/x-rst
Created: 18-Jun-2009
Post-History: 19-Jun-2009, 12-Jun-2020


Abstract
========

This PEP outlines Python's backwards compatibility policy.


Rationale
=========

As one of the most used programming languages today [#tiobe]_, the
Python core language and its standard library play a critical role in
millions of applications and libraries. This is fantastic. However, it
means the development team must be very careful not to break this
existing 3rd party code with new releases.

This PEP takes the perspective that "backwards incompatibility" means
preexisting code ceases to comparatively function after a change. It is
acknowledged that this is not a concrete definition, but the expectation
is people in general understand what is meant by
"backwards incompatibility", and if they are unsure they may ask the
Python development team and/or steering council for guidance.


Backwards Compatibility Rules
=============================

This policy applies to all public APIs.  These include:

- Syntax and behavior of these constructs as defined by the reference
  manual.

- The C-API.

- Function, class, module, attribute, and method names and types.

- Given a set of arguments, the return value, side effects, and raised
  exceptions of a function.  This does not preclude changes from
  reasonable bug fixes.

- The position and expected types of arguments and returned values.

- Behavior of classes with regards to subclasses: the conditions under
  which overridden methods are called.

- Documented exceptions and the semantics which lead to their raising.

- Exceptions commonly raised in EAFP scenarios.

Others are explicitly not part of the public API.  They can change or
be removed at any time in any way.  These include:

- Function, class, module, attribute, method, and C-API names and
  types that are prefixed by "_" (except special names).

- Anything documented publicly as being private.

- Imported modules (unless explicitly documented as part of the public
  API; e.g. importing the ``bacon`` module in the ``spam`` does not
  automatically mean ``spam.bacon`` is part of the public API unless
  it is documented as such).

- Inheritance patterns of internal classes.

- Test suites.  (Anything in the ``Lib/test`` directory or test
  subdirectories of packages.)

- Backward compatibility rules do not apply to any module or API that is
  explicitly documented as **Provisional** per PEP 411.


Basic policy for backwards compatibility
----------------------------------------

* In general, incompatibilities should have a large benefit to
  breakage ratio, and the incompatibility should be easy to resolve in
  affected code.  For example, adding an stdlib module with the same
  name as a third party package is generally not acceptable.  Adding
  a method or attribute that conflicts with 3rd party code through
  inheritance, however, is likely reasonable.

* Unless it is going through the deprecation process below, the
  behavior of an API *must* not change in an incompatible fashion
  between any two consecutive releases.  Python's yearly release
  process (:pep:`602`) means that the deprecation period must last at
  least two years.

* Similarly a feature cannot be removed without notice between any two
  consecutive releases.

* The steering council may grant exceptions to this policy. In
  particular, they may shorten the required deprecation period for a
  feature. Exceptions are only granted for extreme situations such as
  dangerously broken or insecure features or features no one could
  reasonably be depending on (e.g., support for completely obsolete
  platforms).


Making Incompatible Changes
===========================

Making an incompatible change is a gradual process performed over
several releases:

1. Discuss the change.  Depending on the degree of incompatibility,
   this could be on the bug tracker, python-dev, python-list, or the
   appropriate SIG.  A PEP or similar document may be written.
   Hopefully users of the affected API will pipe up to comment.

2. Add a warning.  If behavior is changing, the API may gain a new
   function or method to perform the new behavior; old usage should
   raise the warning.  If an API is being removed, simply warn
   whenever it is entered.  ``DeprecationWarning`` is the usual
   warning category to use, but ``PendingDeprecationWarning`` may be
   used in special cases where the old and new versions of the API will
   coexist for many releases [#warnings]_. Compiler warnings are also
   acceptable. The warning message should include the release the
   incompatibility is expected to become the default and a link to an
   issue that users can post feedback to.

3. Wait for the warning to appear in at least two major Python
   versions. It's fine to wait more than two releases.

4. See if there's any feedback.  Users not involved in the original
   discussions may comment now after seeing the warning.  Perhaps
   reconsider.

5. The behavior change or feature removal may now be made default or
   permanent having reached the declared version. Remove the old
   version and warning.


References
==========

.. [#tiobe] TIOBE Programming Community Index

   http://www.tiobe.com/index.php/content/paperinfo/tpci/index.html

.. [#warnings] The warnings module

   http://docs.python.org/library/warnings.html

# Compatibility policy context

## Scope and evidence boundary

This workspace records Python's upstream backwards compatibility policy, not a
downstream implementation. The evaluation cutoff is **2020-07-20**, the only
snapshot date in the [evidence index](evidence/index.txt); it is not a claim about
policy today. The index supplies the upstream revision and SHA-256, which matches
the local snapshot.

The authoritative local source for the requirements below is
[PEP 387, Backwards Compatibility Policy](evidence/compatibility-2020-07-20.rst).
Section names in citations refer to that unchanged source. Its header identifies
it as **Active**, **Process**, authored by Benjamin Peterson, with Brett Cannon
as BDFL-Delegate on behalf of the steering council. This establishes upstream
policy status; the packet supplies no downstream adoption, runtime verification,
or feature-specific exception approval.

Read [compatibility scope](#compatibility-scope), then the
[change procedure](#deprecation-and-incompatible-changes). Check
[unresolved questions](#unresolved-questions) before applying timing rules.

## Compatibility scope

The policy protects all public APIs, including:

- Reference-manual syntax and behavior, and the C API.
- Function, class, module, attribute, and method names and types.
- Return values, side effects, and raised exceptions for given arguments;
  reasonable bug fixes are not precluded.
- Argument and return-value positions and expected types.
- Subclass behavior, including when overridden methods are called.
- Documented exceptions and their triggering semantics, and exceptions commonly
  raised in EAFP scenarios.

The following are explicitly outside the protected public API and may change or
be removed at any time: underscore-prefixed names and types (except special
names), anything publicly documented as private, imported modules unless
explicitly documented as public API, internal-class inheritance patterns, and
test suites (`Lib/test` and package test subdirectories). Importing `bacon` inside
`spam` alone does not make `spam.bacon` public. Compatibility rules also do not
apply to modules or APIs explicitly documented as **Provisional** under PEP 411.

Source: PEP 387, “Backwards Compatibility Rules.”

## Decisions, rationale, and authority

- **Active upstream policy:** incompatible changes should offer a large benefit
  relative to breakage and be easy to accommodate. Protecting the many existing
  applications and libraries is the rationale. A new standard-library module
  colliding with a third-party package name is generally unacceptable; a new
  method or attribute conflicting through inheritance is likely reasonable.
- API behavior **must not** change incompatibly between consecutive releases
  without the deprecation process. Features likewise cannot be removed without
  notice between consecutive releases.
- **Exception authority:** the steering council may grant exceptions, including
  shorter deprecation periods, only for extreme situations such as dangerously
  broken or insecure features, or features nobody could reasonably depend on
  (for example, completely obsolete platform support). These examples do not
  themselves constitute approval for a particular change.
- The rationale describes incompatibility as preexisting code ceasing to
  comparatively function after a change, acknowledging that this is not a
  concrete definition. Seek guidance from Python developers and/or the steering
  council when classification is unclear.

Sources: PEP 387, “Rationale” and “Basic policy for backwards compatibility.”

## Deprecation and incompatible changes

The basic policy explicitly requires **at least two years** of deprecation in
light of Python's yearly release process (PEP 602). The numbered procedure also
requires the warning to appear in **at least two major Python versions** and
permits waiting longer. These are distinct formulations; the unresolved timing
issue below must remain visible.

1. Discuss the change on an appropriate bug tracker, mailing list, or SIG,
   depending on its incompatibility. A PEP or similar document may be written;
   affected users should have an opportunity to comment.
2. Add a warning. For changed behavior, a new function or method may provide the
   new behavior while old usage warns. For removal, warn whenever the API is
   entered. Normally use `DeprecationWarning`; special cases in which old and new
   APIs coexist for many releases may use `PendingDeprecationWarning`. Compiler
   warnings are acceptable too. The warning message should name the release
   when the incompatibility is expected to become the default and link to an
   issue where users can give feedback.
3. Wait for warning exposure in at least two major Python versions, retaining
   the separate two-year requirement stated in the basic policy.
4. Review feedback, including from users reached only by the warning, and
   reconsider the change if warranted.
5. Once the declared version has been reached and the process completed, make
   the behavior change or removal default or permanent; remove the old version
   and warning.

Source: PEP 387, “Basic policy for backwards compatibility” and “Making
Incompatible Changes.” No feature-specific schedule is supplied.

## Historical continuity and supersession

The source header records creation on **2009-06-18** and post-history entries
**2009-06-19** and **2020-06-12**. Those dates do not provide the contents of
earlier policy revisions. The supplied 2020 snapshot explicitly ties its
two-year minimum to the yearly release process, while retaining the procedure's
version-count wording. Preserve both statements and that rationale; the packet
does not establish which wording changed when or that one supersedes the other.

Only one snapshot is supplied, so no earlier-to-later policy replacement can be
verified. No older policy is separately operative in this context. If additional
authorized evidence arrives, update the affected requirements in place and
retain significant earlier decisions, rationale, dates, and citations with an
explicit superseded status and a link to their replacement.

Sources: PEP 387 header and timing sections; evidence index.

## Unresolved questions

| Issue | Evidence and consequence | Needed resolution |
| --- | --- | --- |

# Compatibility policy context

## Scope and evidence boundary

This workspace records Python's upstream backwards compatibility policy, not a
downstream implementation. The evaluation cutoff is **2020-07-20**, the only
snapshot date in the [evidence index](evidence/index.txt); it is not a claim about
policy today. The index supplies the upstream revision and SHA-256, which matches
the local snapshot.

The authoritative local source for the requirements below is
[PEP 387, Backwards Compatibility Policy](evidence/compatibility-2020-07-20.rst).
Section names in citations refer to that unchanged source. Its header identifies
it as **Active**, **Process**, authored by Benjamin Peterson, with Brett Cannon
as BDFL-Delegate on behalf of the steering council. This establishes upstream
policy status; the packet supplies no downstream adoption, runtime verification,
or feature-specific exception approval.

Read [compatibility scope](#compatibility-scope), then the
[change procedure](#deprecation-and-incompatible-changes). Check
[unresolved questions](#unresolved-questions) before applying timing rules.

## Compatibility scope

The policy protects all public APIs, including:

- Reference-manual syntax and behavior, and the C API.
- Function, class, module, attribute, and method names and types.
- Return values, side effects, and raised exceptions for given arguments;
  reasonable bug fixes are not precluded.
- Argument and return-value positions and expected types.
- Subclass behavior, including when overridden methods are called.
- Documented exceptions and their triggering semantics, and exceptions commonly
  raised in EAFP scenarios.

The following are explicitly outside the protected public API and may change or
be removed at any time: underscore-prefixed names and types (except special
names), anything publicly documented as private, imported modules unless
explicitly documented as public API, internal-class inheritance patterns, and
test suites (`Lib/test` and package test subdirectories). Importing `bacon` inside
`spam` alone does not make `spam.bacon` public. Compatibility rules also do not
apply to modules or APIs explicitly documented as **Provisional** under PEP 411.

Source: PEP 387, “Backwards Compatibility Rules.”

## Decisions, rationale, and authority

- **Active upstream policy:** incompatible changes should offer a large benefit
  relative to breakage and be easy to accommodate. Protecting the many existing
  applications and libraries is the rationale. A new standard-library module
  colliding with a third-party package name is generally unacceptable; a new
  method or attribute conflicting through inheritance is likely reasonable.
- API behavior **must not** change incompatibly between consecutive releases
  without the deprecation process. Features likewise cannot be removed without
  notice between consecutive releases.
- **Exception authority:** the steering council may grant exceptions, including
  shorter deprecation periods, only for extreme situations such as dangerously
  broken or insecure features, or features nobody could reasonably depend on
  (for example, completely obsolete platform support). These examples do not
  themselves constitute approval for a particular change.
- The rationale describes incompatibility as preexisting code ceasing to
  comparatively function after a change, acknowledging that this is not a
  concrete definition. Seek guidance from Python developers and/or the steering
  council when classification is unclear.

Sources: PEP 387, “Rationale” and “Basic policy for backwards compatibility.”

## Deprecation and incompatible changes

The basic policy explicitly requires **at least two years** of deprecation in
light of Python's yearly release process (PEP 602). The numbered procedure also
requires the warning to appear in **at least two major Python versions** and
permits waiting longer. These are distinct formulations; the unresolved timing
issue below must remain visible.

1. Discuss the change on an appropriate bug tracker, mailing list, or SIG,
   depending on its incompatibility. A PEP or similar document may be written;
   affected users should have an opportunity to comment.
2. Add a warning. For changed behavior, a new function or method may provide the
   new behavior while old usage warns. For removal, warn whenever the API is
   entered. Normally use `DeprecationWarning`; special cases in which old and new
   APIs coexist for many releases may use `PendingDeprecationWarning`. Compiler
   warnings are acceptable too. The warning message should name the release
   when the incompatibility is expected to become the default and link to an
   issue where users can give feedback.
3. Wait for warning exposure in at least two major Python versions, retaining
   the separate two-year requirement stated in the basic policy.
4. Review feedback, including from users reached only by the warning, and
   reconsider the change if warranted.
5. Once the declared version has been reached and the process completed, make
   the behavior change or removal default or permanent; remove the old version
   and warning.

Incompatible Changes.” No feature-specific schedule is supplied.

earlier policy revisions. The supplied 2020 snapshot explicitly ties its

PEP: 387
Title: Backwards Compatibility Policy
Version: $Revision$
Last-Modified: $Date$
Author: Benjamin Peterson <benjamin@python.org>
BDFL-Delegate: Brett Cannon (on behalf of the steering council)
Discussions-To: https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-387-backwards-compatibilty-policy/
Status: Active
Type: Process
Content-Type: text/x-rst
Created: 18-Jun-2009
Post-History: 19-Jun-2009, 12-Jun-2020


Abstract
========

This PEP outlines Python's backwards compatibility policy.


Rationale
=========

As one of the most used programming languages today [#tiobe]_, the
Python core language and its standard library play a critical role in
millions of applications and libraries. This is fantastic. However, it
means the development team must be very careful not to break this
existing 3rd party code with new releases.

This PEP takes the perspective that "backwards incompatibility" means
preexisting code ceases to comparatively function after a change. It is
acknowledged that this is not a concrete definition, but the expectation
is people in general understand what is meant by
"backwards incompatibility", and if they are unsure they may ask the
Python development team and/or steering council for guidance.


Backwards Compatibility Rules
=============================

This policy applies to all public APIs.  These include:

- Syntax and behavior of these constructs as defined by the reference
  manual.

- The C-API.

- Function, class, module, attribute, and method names and types.

- Given a set of arguments, the return value, side effects, and raised
  exceptions of a function.  This does not preclude changes from
  reasonable bug fixes.

- The position and expected types of arguments and returned values.

- Behavior of classes with regards to subclasses: the conditions under
  which overridden methods are called.

- Documented exceptions and the semantics which lead to their raising.

- Exceptions commonly raised in EAFP scenarios.

Others are explicitly not part of the public API.  They can change or
be removed at any time in any way.  These include:

- Function, class, module, attribute, method, and C-API names and
  types that are prefixed by "_" (except special names).

- Anything documented publicly as being private.

- Imported modules (unless explicitly documented as part of the public
  API; e.g. importing the ``bacon`` module in the ``spam`` does not
  automatically mean ``spam.bacon`` is part of the public API unless
  it is documented as such).

- Inheritance patterns of internal classes.

- Test suites.  (Anything in the ``Lib/test`` directory or test
  subdirectories of packages.)

- Backward compatibility rules do not apply to any module or API that is
  explicitly documented as **Provisional** per PEP 411.


Basic policy for backwards compatibility
----------------------------------------

* In general, incompatibilities should have a large benefit to
  breakage ratio, and the incompatibility should be easy to resolve in
  affected code.  For example, adding an stdlib module with the same
  name as a third party package is generally not acceptable.  Adding
  a method or attribute that conflicts with 3rd party code through
  inheritance, however, is likely reasonable.

* Unless it is going through the deprecation process below, the
  behavior of an API *must* not change in an incompatible fashion
  between any two consecutive releases.  Python's yearly release
  process (:pep:`602`) means that the deprecation period must last at
  least two years.

* Similarly a feature cannot be removed without notice between any two
  consecutive releases.

* The steering council may grant exceptions to this policy. In
  particular, they may shorten the required deprecation period for a
  feature. Exceptions are only granted for extreme situations such as
  dangerously broken or insecure features or features no one could
  reasonably be depending on (e.g., support for completely obsolete
  platforms).


Making Incompatible Changes
===========================

Making an incompatible change is a gradual process performed over
several releases:

1. Discuss the change.  Depending on the degree of incompatibility,
   this could be on the bug tracker, python-dev, python-list, or the
   appropriate SIG.  A PEP or similar document may be written.
   Hopefully users of the affected API will pipe up to comment.

2. Add a warning.  If behavior is changing, the API may gain a new
   function or method to perform the new behavior; old usage should
   raise the warning.  If an API is being removed, simply warn
   whenever it is entered.  ``DeprecationWarning`` is the usual
   warning category to use, but ``PendingDeprecationWarning`` may be
   used in special cases where the old and new versions of the API will
   coexist for many releases [#warnings]_. Compiler warnings are also
   acceptable. The warning message should include the release the
   incompatibility is expected to become the default and a link to an
   issue that users can post feedback to.

3. Wait for the warning to appear in at least two major Python
   versions. It's fine to wait more than two releases.

4. See if there's any feedback.  Users not involved in the original
   discussions may comment now after seeing the warning.  Perhaps
   reconsider.

5. The behavior change or feature removal may now be made default or
   permanent having reached the declared version. Remove the old
   version and warning.


References
==========

.. [#tiobe] TIOBE Programming Community Index

   http://www.tiobe.com/index.php/content/paperinfo/tpci/index.html

.. [#warnings] The warnings module

   http://docs.python.org/library/warnings.html


Copyright
=========

This document has been placed in the public domain.
