PEP: 602
Title: Annual Release Cycle for Python
Version: $Revision$
Last-Modified: $Date$
Author: Łukasz Langa <lukasz@python.org>
BDFL-Delegate: Brett Cannon (on behalf of the steering council)
Discussions-To: https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-602-annual-release-cycle-for-python/2296/
Status: Accepted
Type: Informational
Content-Type: text/x-rst
Created: 04-Jun-2019
Python-Version: 3.9


Abstract
========

This document describes a change in the release calendar for Python
starting with Python 3.9.  This change accelerates the release cadence
such that major versions are released predictably every twelve months,
in October every year.


Implementation
==============

Seventeen months to develop a major version
-------------------------------------------

This PEP proposes that Python 3.X.0 will be developed for around
17 months:

- The first *five months* overlap with Python 3.(X-1).0's beta
  and release candidate stages and are thus unversioned.

- The next *seven months* are spent on versioned alpha releases where
  both new features are incrementally added and bug fixes are included.

- The following *three months* are spent on four versioned beta releases
  where **no new features** can be added but bug fixes are still
  included.

- The final *two months* are spent on two release candidates (or more,
  if necessary) and conclude with the release of the final release of
  Python 3.X.0.

1½ year of full support, 3½ more years of security fixes
--------------------------------------------------------

After the release of Python 3.X.0, the 3.X series is maintained for
five years:

- During the *first eighteen months* (1½ year) it receives bugfix
  updates and full releases (sources and installers for Windows and
  macOS) are made approximately every other month.

- For the next *forty two months* (3½ years) it receives security
  updates and source-only releases are made on an as-needed basis
  (no fixed cadence).

- The final source-only release is made *five years* after 3.X.0.

Annual release cadence
----------------------

Feature development of Python 3.(X+1).0 starts as soon as
Python 3.X.0 Beta 1 is released.  This creates a twelve month delta
between major Python versions.


Example
=======

- 3.9 development begins: Tuesday, 2019-06-04
- 3.9.0 alpha 1: Monday, 2019-10-14
- 3.9.0 alpha 2: Monday, 2019-11-18
- 3.9.0 alpha 3: Monday, 2019-12-16
- 3.9.0 alpha 4: Monday, 2020-01-13
- 3.9.0 alpha 5: Monday, 2020-02-17
- 3.9.0 alpha 6: Monday, 2020-03-16
- 3.9.0 alpha 7: Monday, 2020-04-13
- 3.9.0 beta 1: Monday, 2020-05-18
  (No new features beyond this point.)

- 3.9.0 beta 2: Monday, 2020-06-08
- 3.9.0 beta 3: Monday, 2020-06-29
- 3.9.0 beta 4: Monday, 2020-07-20
- 3.9.0 candidate 1: Monday, 2020-08-10
- 3.9.0 candidate 2: Monday, 2020-09-14
- 3.9.0 final: Monday, 2020-10-05

.. figure:: pep-0602-example-release-calendar.png
   :align: center
   :width: 100%

   Figure 1. Consequences of the annual release cycle on the calendar.

In comparison, if this PEP is rejected and Python keeps the current
release schedule:

- 3.9 development begins: Tuesday, 2019-06-04
- 3.9.0 alpha 1: Monday, 2020-08-03  (10 months later)
- 3.9.0 alpha 2: Monday, 2020-09-07
- 3.9.0 alpha 3: Monday, 2020-10-05
- 3.9.0 alpha 4: Monday, 2020-11-02
- 3.9.0 beta 1: Monday, 2020-11-30  (6 months later)
- 3.9.0 beta 2: Monday, 2021-01-04
- 3.9.0 beta 3: Monday, 2021-02-01
- 3.9.0 beta 4: Monday, 2021-03-01
- 3.9.0 candidate 1: Monday, 2021-03-29
- 3.9.0 candidate 2: Monday, 2021-04-05 (if necessary)
- 3.9.0 final: Monday, 2021-04-19  (6 months later)


Dependent Policies
==================

Deprecations
------------

The current policy around breaking changes assumes at least two releases
before a deprecated feature is removed from Python or a ``__future__``
behavior is enabled by default.  This is documented in PEP 387.

This PEP proposes to keep this policy of **at least** two releases
before making a breaking change.

The term of the Steering Council
--------------------------------

The current wording of PEP 13 states that "a new council is elected
after each feature release".  This PEP proposes to keep this policy
as it will lead to a consistent election schedule.

The term of the Release Manager
-------------------------------

The current undocumented convention is for a single Release Manager to
handle two feature releases of Python.  This PEP proposes to keep this
policy, allowing for the term to be extended to more releases with
approval from the Steering Council and the Cabal of Release Managers.

In particular, since this PEP is authored by the active Release Manager
and its effect would shorten the term of the Release Manager, the author
is open to managing the release of a third feature release to compensate
for the disruption.


Rationale and Goals
===================

This change provides the following advantages:

- makes releases smaller: since doubling the cadence doesn't double our
  available development resources, consecutive releases are going to be
  smaller in terms of features;

- puts features and bug fixes in hands of users sooner;

- creates a more gradual upgrade path for users, by decreasing the
  surface of change in any single release;

- creates a predictable calendar for releases where the final release is
  always in October (so after the annual core sprint), and the beta
  phase starts in late May (so after PyCon US sprints), which is
  especially important for core developers who need to plan to include
  Python involvement in their calendar;

- decreases the urge to rush features shortly before "Beta 1" due to
  the risk of them "slipping for 18 months";

- allows for synchronizing the schedule of Python release management
  with external distributors like Fedora who've been historically very
  helpful in finding regressions early not only in core Python but also
  in third-party libraries, helping moving the community forward to
  support the latest version of Python from Day 1;

- increases the explicit alpha release phase, which provides meaningful
  snapshots of progress on new features;

- significantly cuts the implicit "alpha 0" release phase which provides
  limited use for new development anyway (it overlaps with the beta of
  the *currently developed*, still unreleased, version).

Non-goals
---------

Adopting an annual release calendar allows for natural switching to
calendar versioning, for example by calling Python 3.9 "Python 3.20"
since it's released in October '20 and so on ("Python 3.23" would be the
one released in October '23).

While the ease of switching to calendar versioning can be treated as
an advantage of an annual release cycle, this PEP does not advocate for
or against a change in how Python is versioned.  Should the annual
release cycle be adopted, the versioning question will be dealt with in
a separate PEP.

Non-risks
---------

This change does not shorten the currently documented support calendar
for a Python release, both in terms of bugfix releases and security
fixes.

This change does not accelerate the velocity of development.  Python is
not going to become incompatible faster or accrue new features faster.
It's just that features are going to be released more gradually as they
are developed.

Consequently, while this change introduces the ability for users to
upgrade much faster, it does not require them to do so.  Say, if they
upgrade every second release, their experience with Python is going to
be similar to the current situation.

Risks
-----

Python redistribution
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

This requires changes to how integrators, like Linux distributions,
release Python within their systems.

The testing matrix
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

This eventually increases the testing matrix for library and application
maintainers that want to support all actively supported Python versions
by one or two:

.. figure:: pep-0602-overlapping-support-matrix.png
   :align: center
   :width: 50%

   Figure 2. Testing matrix in the 18-month cadence vs. the 12-month

The "extended bugfix support at the discretion of the Release Manager"
stage of the current release cycle is not codified.  If fact, PEP 101
currently states that after the release of Python 3.(X+1).0 only one
last bugfix release is made for Python 3.X.0.  However, in practice at
least the last four versions of Python 3 overlapped with stable releases
of the next version for around six months.  Figure 2 is including
this information to demonstrate that overlap between stable version
releases with the 12-month release cadence will be nothing new.

Other policies may depend on the release cadence
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Although identified dependent policies were addressed in a previous
section, it is entirely possible there are some other areas which
implicitly rely on the timing of Python releases.


Rejected Ideas
--------------

Keep the current 18 month release cadence
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

This is undesirable both for core developers and end users. From the
perspective of the core developer:

- it makes contribution scheduling harder due to irregular release
  dates every year;

- it creates a surge of rushed commits before (and even after!) Beta 1
  due to the stress involved with "missing a release";

- ironically, after Beta 1 it creates a false sense of having "plenty of
  time" before the next release, time that passes quickly regardless;

- it causes certain elements of the workflow to be executed so rarely
  that they are not explicitly documented, let alone automated.

More importantly, from the perspective of the user:

- it creates releases with many new features, some being explicitly
  incompatible and some being accidentally incompatible, which makes
  the upgrade cost relatively high every time;

- it sits on features and incompatible bug fixes for over a year before
  becoming available to the user; and more specifically

- it causes every "point zero" release to be extra risky for users.
  While we provide and recommend testing with alphas and betas,
  "point zero" is the first release of a given Python version for many
  users.  The bigger a release is feature-wise, the more potential
  problems are hiding in "point zero releases".

Double the release cadence to achieve 9 months between major versions
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

This was originally proposed in PEP 596 and rejected as both too
irregular and too short.  This would not give any of the benefits of
a regular release calendar but it would shorten all development phases,
especially the beta + RC phases.  This was considered dangerous.

Keep "4 betas over 4 months and a final month for the release candidate"
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

While this would make the release calendar a bit cleaner, `it would make
it very hard for external distributors like Fedora
<https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-602-annual-release-cycle-for-python/2296/79?u=ambv>`_
to release the newest version of Python as soon as possible.  We are
adjusting Python's calendar here in the hope that this will enable
Fedora to integrate the newest version of Python with the newest version
of Fedora *as both are being developed* which makes both projects
better.

Slow down releases but don't freeze feature development with Beta 1
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

This is described in PEP 598.  This proposal includes non-standard
concepts like the "incremental feature release" which makes it hard
to understand.  The presented advantages are unclear while the
unfamiliarity of the scheme poses a real risk of user and integrator
confusion.

Long-Term Support Releases
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Each version of Python is effectively long-term support: it's supported
for five years, with the first eighteen months allowing regular bug
fixes and security updates.  For the remaining time security updates are
accepted and promptly released.

No extended support in the vein of Python 2.7 is planned going forward.

PEP: 602
Title: Annual Release Cycle for Python
Author: Łukasz Langa <lukasz@python.org>
PEP-Delegate: Brett Cannon <brett@python.org>
Discussions-To: https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-602-annual-release-cycle-for-python/2296/
Status: Active
Type: Process
Created: 04-Jun-2019
Python-Version: 3.9
Post-History: `09-Oct-2023 <https://discuss.python.org/t/27002>`__
Resolution: https://mail.python.org/archives/list/python-dev@python.org/thread/KE7OS4PZASZMFTW2FP2MWZU5R4Q2QZKU/


Abstract
========

This document describes a change in the release calendar for Python
starting with Python 3.9.  This change accelerates the release cadence
such that feature versions are released predictably every twelve months,
in October every year.


Implementation
==============

Seventeen months to develop a feature version
---------------------------------------------

This PEP proposes that Python 3.X.0 will be developed for around
17 months:

- The first *five months* overlap with Python 3.(X-1).0's beta
  and release candidate stages and are thus unversioned.

- The next *seven months* are spent on versioned alpha releases where
  both new features are incrementally added and bug fixes are included.

- The following *three months* are spent on four versioned beta releases
  where **no new features** can be added but bug fixes are still
  included.

- The final *two months* are spent on two release candidates (or more,
  if necessary) and conclude with the release of the final release of
  Python 3.X.0.

2 years of full support, 3 more years of security fixes
-------------------------------------------------------

After the release of Python 3.X.0, the 3.X series is maintained for
five years:

- During the *first twenty four months* (2 years) it receives bugfix
  updates and full releases (sources and installers for Windows and
  macOS) are made approximately every other month.

- For the next *thirty six months* (3 years) it receives security
  updates and source-only releases are made on an as-needed basis
  (no fixed cadence).

- The final source-only release is made *five years* after 3.X.0.

Note: 2 years of full support start with
:pep:`Python 3.13 <719>`.  Python versions
3.9 - 3.12 operate on a calendar with 1½ year of full support, followed
by 3½ more years of security fixes.


Annual release cadence
----------------------

Feature development of Python 3.(X+1).0 starts as soon as
Python 3.X.0 Beta 1 is released.  This creates a twelve-month delta
between Python feature versions.


Example
=======

- 3.9 development begins: Tuesday, 2019-06-04
- 3.9.0 alpha 1: Monday, 2019-10-14
- 3.9.0 alpha 2: Monday, 2019-11-18
- 3.9.0 alpha 3: Monday, 2019-12-16
- 3.9.0 alpha 4: Monday, 2020-01-13
- 3.9.0 alpha 5: Monday, 2020-02-17
- 3.9.0 alpha 6: Monday, 2020-03-16
- 3.9.0 alpha 7: Monday, 2020-04-13
- 3.9.0 beta 1: Monday, 2020-05-18
  (No new features beyond this point.)

- 3.9.0 beta 2: Monday, 2020-06-08
- 3.9.0 beta 3: Monday, 2020-06-29
- 3.9.0 beta 4: Monday, 2020-07-20
- 3.9.0 candidate 1: Monday, 2020-08-10
- 3.9.0 candidate 2: Monday, 2020-09-14
- 3.9.0 final: Monday, 2020-10-05

.. figure:: pep-0602-example-release-calendar.png
   :align: center
   :width: 100%

   Figure 1. Consequences of the annual release cycle on the calendar.

In comparison, if this PEP is rejected and Python keeps the current
release schedule:

- 3.9 development begins: Tuesday, 2019-06-04
- 3.9.0 alpha 1: Monday, 2020-08-03  (10 months later)
- 3.9.0 alpha 2: Monday, 2020-09-07
- 3.9.0 alpha 3: Monday, 2020-10-05
- 3.9.0 alpha 4: Monday, 2020-11-02
- 3.9.0 beta 1: Monday, 2020-11-30  (6 months later)
- 3.9.0 beta 2: Monday, 2021-01-04
- 3.9.0 beta 3: Monday, 2021-02-01
- 3.9.0 beta 4: Monday, 2021-03-01
- 3.9.0 candidate 1: Monday, 2021-03-29
- 3.9.0 candidate 2: Monday, 2021-04-05 (if necessary)
- 3.9.0 final: Monday, 2021-04-19  (6 months later)


Dependent Policies
==================

Deprecations
------------

The current policy around breaking changes assumes at least two releases
before a deprecated feature is removed from Python or a ``__future__``
behavior is enabled by default.  This is documented in :pep:`387`.

This PEP proposes to keep this policy of **at least** two releases
before making a breaking change.

The term of the Steering Council
--------------------------------

The current wording of :pep:`13` states that "a new council is elected
after each feature release".  This PEP proposes to keep this policy
as it will lead to a consistent election schedule.

The term of the Release Manager
-------------------------------

The current undocumented convention is for a single Release Manager to
handle two feature releases of Python.  This PEP proposes to keep this
policy, allowing for the term to be extended to more releases with
approval from the Steering Council and the Cabal of Release Managers.

In particular, since this PEP is authored by the active Release Manager
and its effect would shorten the term of the Release Manager, the author
is open to managing the release of a third feature release to compensate
for the disruption.


Rationale and Goals
===================

This change provides the following advantages:

- makes releases smaller: since doubling the cadence doesn't double our
  available development resources, consecutive releases are going to be
  smaller in terms of features;

- puts features and bug fixes in hands of users sooner;

- creates a more gradual upgrade path for users, by decreasing the
  surface of change in any single release;

- creates a predictable calendar for releases where the final release is
  always in October (so after the annual core sprint), and the beta
  phase starts in late May (so after PyCon US sprints), which is
  especially important for core developers who need to plan to include
  Python involvement in their calendar;

- decreases the urge to rush features shortly before "Beta 1" due to
  the risk of them "slipping for 18 months";

- allows for synchronizing the schedule of Python release management
  with external distributors like Fedora who've been historically very
  helpful in finding regressions early not only in core Python but also
  in third-party libraries, helping moving the community forward to
  support the latest version of Python from Day 1;

- increases the explicit alpha release phase, which provides meaningful
  snapshots of progress on new features;

- significantly cuts the implicit "alpha 0" release phase which provides
  limited use for new development anyway (it overlaps with the beta of
  the *currently developed*, still unreleased, version).

Non-goals
---------

Adopting an annual release calendar allows for natural switching to
calendar versioning, for example by calling Python 3.9 "Python 3.20"
since it's released in October '20 and so on ("Python 3.23" would be the
one released in October '23).

While the ease of switching to calendar versioning can be treated as
an advantage of an annual release cycle, this PEP does not advocate for
or against a change in how Python is versioned.  Should the annual
release cycle be adopted, the versioning question will be dealt with in
a separate PEP.

Non-risks
---------

This change does not shorten the currently documented support calendar
for a Python release, both in terms of bugfix releases and security
fixes.

This change does not accelerate the velocity of development.  Python is
not going to become incompatible faster or accrue new features faster.
It's just that features are going to be released more gradually as they
are developed.

Consequently, while this change introduces the ability for users to
upgrade much faster, it does not require them to do so.  Say, if they
upgrade every second release, their experience with Python is going to
be similar to the current situation.

Risks
-----

Python redistribution
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

This requires changes to how integrators, like Linux distributions,
release Python within their systems.

The testing matrix
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

This eventually increases the testing matrix for library and application
maintainers that want to support all actively supported Python versions
by one or two:

.. figure:: pep-0602-overlapping-support-matrix.png
   :align: center
   :width: 50%

   Figure 2. Testing matrix in the 18-month cadence vs. the 12-month

The "extended bugfix support at the discretion of the Release Manager"
stage of the current release cycle is not codified.  If fact, :pep:`101`
currently states that after the release of Python 3.(X+1).0 only one
last bugfix release is made for Python 3.X.0.  However, in practice at
least the last four versions of Python 3 overlapped with stable releases

releases with the 12-month release cadence will be nothing new.

Other policies may depend on the release cadence
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

section, it is entirely possible there are some other areas which
implicitly rely on the timing of Python releases.


Rejected Ideas
--------------

Keep the current 18 month release cadence
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

This is undesirable both for core developers and end users. From the
perspective of the core developer:

- it makes contribution scheduling harder due to irregular release
  dates every year;

- it creates a surge of rushed commits before (and even after!) Beta 1

- ironically, after Beta 1 it creates a false sense of having "plenty of

- it causes certain elements of the workflow to be executed so rarely
  that they are not explicitly documented, let alone automated.

More importantly, from the perspective of the user:

- it creates releases with many new features, some being explicitly
  incompatible and some being accidentally incompatible, which makes
  the upgrade cost relatively high every time;

- it sits on features and incompatible bug fixes for over a year before
  becoming available to the user; and more specifically

- it causes every "point zero" release to be extra risky for users.

  "point zero" is the first release of a given Python version for many
  users.  The bigger a release is feature-wise, the more potential
  problems are hiding in "point zero releases".

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

irregular and too short.  This would not give any of the benefits of

especially the beta + RC phases.  This was considered dangerous.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

# Release policy context

## Scope and authority

This workspace records upstream Python release-policy history. The evidence cutoff
is **2019-09-10**, not today's policy. The [evidence index](evidence/index.txt)
supplies one revision of [PEP 602](evidence/releases-2019-09-10.rst), *Annual Release
Cycle for Python*, authored by Łukasz Langa, created 2019-06-04, marked
**Draft / Informational**, and targeting Python 3.9. The index records the upstream
revision and SHA-256 for provenance.

The rules below are **proposed at this cutoff**, not evidence of acceptance or
implementation. The packet supplies no downstream adoption, runtime observations,
or feature-specific exception approvals. The source's “Implementation” heading
does not establish implementation. PEPs 596 and 598 are described only through
this snapshot; their own texts are not supplied.

Read [timing](#proposed-release-and-support-timing), then
[decision history](#rationale-and-historical-alternatives),
[dependent rules](#dependent-governance-and-open-exceptions), and
[unresolved evidence](#contradictions-and-verification-limits).

## Proposed release and support timing

Source: PEP 602, **Abstract**, **Implementation**, and **Example** in the
[local snapshot](evidence/releases-2019-09-10.rst).

| Area | Proposed rule |
| --- | --- |
| Release interval | Python 3.X.0 releases every 12 months, starting with 3.9. The source calls these “major” versions. |
| Development overlap | Development of 3.(X+1).0 starts at 3.X.0 Beta 1. The first five months overlap the preceding version's beta/RC stages and are unversioned. |
| Alpha | Seven months of versioned alphas, accepting new features and bug fixes. |
| Beta | Four months of versioned betas; no new features, bug fixes allowed. |
| Release candidate | A final month with one RC or more if needed, ending in the final release. |
| Full support | First year after 3.X.0: approximately monthly bugfix updates; a final 3.X.12 follows 3.(X+1).0 final. |
| Security support | Next four years: security updates with source-only releases as needed, without a monthly cadence. |
| End of support | Final source-only release five years after 3.X.0. |

The intended recurring calendar places finals in October after the annual core
sprint and beta starts in late May after PyCon US sprints. The illustrative 3.9
schedule begins development on 2019-06-04, has seven alphas from 2019-10-14 to
2020-04-13, and freezes features at Beta 1 on 2020-05-18. It lists four betas,
RC 1 on 2020-09-14, optional RC 2 on 2020-09-21, and final on 2020-10-05.
These are an example, not observed releases. Total development duration is
[internally inconsistent](#contradictions-and-verification-limits).

## Rationale and historical alternatives

Source: **Rationale and Goals**, **Non-goals**, **Non-risks**, **Risks**, and
**Rejected Ideas** in [PEP 602](evidence/releases-2019-09-10.rst).

Annual releases aim to deliver smaller changes sooner, reduce upgrade difficulty
and pressure to rush before Beta 1, and provide a predictable calendar. A longer
explicit alpha phase offers useful progress snapshots; a shorter implicit
“alpha 0” reduces time overlapping the preceding unreleased version's beta.
The proposal does not assume more development resources or faster feature growth
or incompatibility. Users need not upgrade every release: every second release
is offered as an experience similar to the then-current cadence. Security support
is not shortened.

| Historical choice | Status and rationale in this draft |
| --- | --- |
| Keep the existing 18-month cadence | Rejected by the proposal: encourages rushed commits before and even after Beta 1, then a false sense of spare time; infrequent workflow steps remain undocumented or unautomated. Larger releases increase upgrade costs, delay features and incompatible bug fixes for over a year, and make point-zero releases riskier for users who skip prerelease testing. |
| Nine-month cadence | Reported as originally proposed in PEP 596 and rejected for irregularity and excessive speed, including a dangerously shortened beta phase. |
| Slower releases without a Beta 1 feature freeze | PEP 598 alternative rejected here: unfamiliar “incremental feature release” concepts are hard to understand, benefits are unclear, and users/integrators may be confused. |

The 12-month proposal would replace the described 18-month baseline **if adopted**.
No supplied later decision establishes that supersession; the baseline is
historical context, not a current instruction for a downstream project. Likewise,
rejection within this draft must not be presented as separately verified approval
by a governing body.

**Versioning is a non-goal.** Calendar names such as Python 3.20 for an October
2020 release (and 3.23 for October 2023) are possibilities, not selected names.
The draft advocates neither for nor against changing version numbering; that
question would require a separate PEP after adoption of the annual calendar.

## Dependent governance and open exceptions

Source: **Risks** in [PEP 602](evidence/releases-2019-09-10.rst).

Adoption would require updates to the deprecation policy, when `__future__`
imports become defaults, Steering Council terms, and Release Manager terms.
The packet supplies no replacement rules or evidence that these updates occurred;
do not infer their durations or translate release counts into elapsed time.

Integrators such as Linux distributions would need to change their release
practices. Supporting every active Python version would eventually enlarge
library/application testing matrices by one or two versions.

The shorter, 12-month bugfix period limits the largest core-maintenance cost so
cadence can increase, but inconveniences users. Making every n-th release an LTS,
in the vein of Python 2.7, is **open for debate**, not an approved exception:
neither n nor LTS support terms are defined. The optional extra RC is an explicit
scheduling allowance; it does not waive the Beta 1 feature freeze. No
feature-specific waiver is supplied.

## Contradictions and verification limits

- **Development duration:** the Implementation heading says “Seventeen months,”
  while its opening sentence says “around 16 months.” The listed phases total
  17 months (5 + 7 + 4 + 1); the example spans roughly 16 months from June 2019
  to October 2020. Preserve this conflict rather than selecting a corrected
  duration. A subsequent authoritative clarification is needed before using
  the total as a scheduling requirement.
- **Calendar precision:** the rationale says beta starts in “late May,” while
  the example specifies May 18. Retain both as stated; no exact recurring
  calendar rule resolving that tension is supplied.
- **Missing figures:** the snapshot references release-calendar and support-matrix
  PNGs absent from the packet. The prose supports the claims above; details of
  those figures cannot be independently checked here.

Future updates should replace affected canonical statements in place, cite newly
supplied authoritative evidence, and retain significant rationale and explicit
supersession. Acceptance status, governance changes, downstream adoption, and
exceptions each need their own evidence; none follows merely from this draft.

| Nine-month cadence | Reported as originally proposed in PEP 596 and rejected for irregularity and excessive speed, including a dangerously shortened beta phase. |
| Slower releases without a Beta 1 feature freeze | PEP 598 alternative rejected here: unfamiliar “incremental feature release” concepts are hard to understand, benefits are unclear, and users/integrators may be confused. |

The 12-month proposal would replace the described 18-month baseline **if adopted**.
No supplied later decision establishes that supersession; the baseline is
historical context, not a current instruction for a downstream project. Likewise,
rejection within this draft must not be presented as separately verified approval
by a governing body.

**Versioning is a non-goal.** Calendar names such as Python 3.20 for an October
2020 release (and 3.23 for October 2023) are possibilities, not selected names.
The draft advocates neither for nor against changing version numbering; that
question would require a separate PEP after adoption of the annual calendar.

## Dependent governance and open exceptions

Source: **Risks** in [PEP 602](evidence/releases-2019-09-10.rst).

Adoption would require updates to the deprecation policy, when `__future__`
imports become defaults, Steering Council terms, and Release Manager terms.
The packet supplies no replacement rules or evidence that these updates occurred;
do not infer their durations or translate release counts into elapsed time.

Integrators such as Linux distributions would need to change their release
practices. Supporting every active Python version would eventually enlarge
library/application testing matrices by one or two versions.

The shorter, 12-month bugfix period limits the largest core-maintenance cost so
cadence can increase, but inconveniences users. Making every n-th release an LTS,
in the vein of Python 2.7, is **open for debate**, not an approved exception:
neither n nor LTS support terms are defined. The optional extra RC is an explicit
scheduling allowance; it does not waive the Beta 1 feature freeze. No
feature-specific waiver is supplied.

## Contradictions and verification limits

- **Development duration:** the Implementation heading says “Seventeen months,”
  while its opening sentence says “around 16 months.” The listed phases total
  17 months (5 + 7 + 4 + 1); the example spans roughly 16 months from June 2019
  to October 2020. Preserve this conflict rather than selecting a corrected
  duration. A subsequent authoritative clarification is needed before using
  the total as a scheduling requirement.
- **Calendar precision:** the rationale says beta starts in “late May,” while
  the example specifies May 18. Retain both as stated; no exact recurring
  calendar rule resolving that tension is supplied.
- **Missing figures:** the snapshot references release-calendar and support-matrix
  PNGs absent from the packet. The prose supports the claims above; details of
  those figures cannot be independently checked here.

Future updates should replace affected canonical statements in place, cite newly
supplied authoritative evidence, and retain significant rationale and explicit
supersession. Acceptance status, governance changes, downstream adoption, and
exceptions each need their own evidence; none follows merely from this draft.

PEP: 602
Title: Annual Release Cycle for Python
Version: $Revision$
Last-Modified: $Date$
Author: Łukasz Langa <lukasz@python.org>
Discussions-To: https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-602-annual-release-cycle-for-python/2296/
Status: Draft
Type: Informational
Content-Type: text/x-rst
Created: 04-Jun-2019
Python-Version: 3.9


Abstract
========

This document describes a change in the release calendar for Python
starting with Python 3.9.  This change accelerates the release cadence
such that major versions are released every twelve months.


Implementation
==============

Seventeen months to develop a major version
-------------------------------------------

This PEP proposes that Python 3.X.0 will be developed for around
16 months:

- The first *five months* overlap with Python 3.(X-1).0's beta
  and release candidate stages and are thus unversioned.

- The next *seven months* are spent on versioned alpha releases where
  both new features are incrementally added and bug fixes are included.

- The following *four months* are spent on versioned beta releases where
  **no new features** can be added but bug fixes are still included.

- The *final month* is spent on a release candidate (or more, if
  necessary) and concludes with the release of the final release of
  Python 3.X.0.

One year of full support, four more years of security fixes
-----------------------------------------------------------

After the relase of Python 3.X.0, the 3.X series is maintained for
five years:

- During the *first year* it receives bugfix updates approximately
  every month.  After the release of 3.(X+1).0 final, a final 3.X.12 is
  released.

- For the next *four years* it receives security updates and
  source-only releases are made on an as-needed basis
  (no monthly cadence).

- The final source-only release is made *five years* after 3.X.0.

Annual release cadence
----------------------

Feature development of Python 3.(X+1).0 starts as soon as
Python 3.X.0 Beta 1 is released.  This creates a twelve month delta
between major Python versions.


Example
=======

- 3.9 development begins: Tuesday, 2019-06-04
- 3.9.0 alpha 1: Monday, 2019-10-14
- 3.9.0 alpha 2: Monday, 2019-11-18
- 3.9.0 alpha 3: Monday, 2019-12-16
- 3.9.0 alpha 4: Monday, 2020-01-13
- 3.9.0 alpha 5: Monday, 2020-02-17
- 3.9.0 alpha 6: Monday, 2020-03-16
- 3.9.0 alpha 7: Monday, 2020-04-13
- 3.9.0 beta 1: Monday, 2020-05-18
  (No new features beyond this point.)

- 3.9.0 beta 2: Monday, 2020-06-15
- 3.9.0 beta 3: Monday, 2020-07-13
- 3.9.0 beta 4: Monday, 2020-08-17
- 3.9.0 candidate 1: Monday, 2020-09-14
- 3.9.0 candidate 2: Monday, 2020-09-21 (if necessary)
- 3.9.0 final: Monday, 2020-10-05

.. figure:: pep-0602-example-release-calendar.png
   :align: center
   :width: 100%

   Figure 1. Consequences of the annual release cycle on the calendar.


Rationale and Goals
===================

This change provides the following advantages:

- makes releases smaller: since doubling the cadence doesn't double our
  available development resources, consecutive releases are going to be
  smaller in terms of features;

- puts features and bug fixes in hands of users sooner;

- creates a more gradual upgrade path for users, by decreasing the
  surface of change in any single release;

- creates a predictable calendar for releases where the final release is
  always in October (so after the annual core sprint), and the beta
  phase starts in late May (so after PyCon US sprints);

- decreases the urge to rush features shortly before "Beta 1" due to
  the risk of them "slipping for 18 months";

- increases the explicit alpha release phase, which provides meaningful
  snapshots of progress on new features;

- significantly cuts the implicit "alpha 0" release phase which provides
  limited use for new development anyway (it overlaps with the beta of
  the *currently developed*, still unreleased, version);

Non-goals
---------

Adopting an annual release calendar allows for natural switching to
calendar versioning, for example by calling Python 3.9 "Python 3.20"
since it's released in October '20 and so on ("Python 3.23" would be the
one released in October '23).

While the ease of switching to calendar versioning can be treated as
an advantage of an annual release cycle, this PEP does not advocate for
or against a change in how Python is versioned.  Should the annual
release cycle be adopted, the versioning question will be dealt with in
a separate PEP.

Non-risks
---------

This change does not shorten the security updates calendar for a Python
release.

This change does not accelerate the velocity of development.  Python is
not going to become incompatible faster or accrue new features faster.
It's just that features are going to be released more gradually as they
are developed.

Consequently, while this change introduces the ability for users to
upgrade much faster, it does not require them to do so.  Say, if they
upgrade every second release, their experience with Python is going to
be very similar to the current situation.

Risks
-----

This requires changes to how integrators, like Linux distributions,
release Python within their systems.

This eventually increases the testing matrix for library and application
maintainers that want to support all actively supported Python versions
by one or two:

.. figure:: pep-0602-overlapping-support-matrix.png
   :align: center
   :width: 100%

   Figure 2. Testing matrix in the 18-month cadence vs. the 12-month

The following policies depend on the release cadence and will have to
be updated:

- the deprecation policy
- the``__future__`` import becoming the default
- the term of the Steering Council
- the term of the Release Manager

Finally, this shortens the bugfix period to twelve months.  This allows
core developers to increase the cadence without increasing the biggest
maintenance cost, however provides an inconvenience to the user.  This
particular risk might be solved by making every n-th release a LTS, in
the vein of Python 2.7.  This is open for debate.

Rejected Ideas
--------------

Keep the current 18 month release cadence
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

This is undesirable both for core developers and end users. From the
perspective of the core developer:

- it creates a surge of rushed commits before (and even after!) Beta 1
  due to the stress involved with "missing a release";

- ironically, after Beta 1 it creates a false sense of having "plenty of
  time" before the next release, time that passes quickly regardless;

- it causes certain elements of the workflow to be executed so rarely
  that they are not explicitly documented, let alone automated.

More importantly, from the perspective of the user:

- it creates releases with many new features, some being explicitly
  incompatible and some being accidentally incompatible, which makes
  the upgrade cost relatively high every time;

- it sits on features and incompatible bug fixes for over a year before
  becoming available to the user; and more specifically

- it causes every "point zero" release to be extra risky for users.
  While we provide and recommend testing with alphas and betas,
  "point zero" is the first release of a given Python version for many
  users.  The bigger a release is feature-wise, the more potential
  problems are hiding in "point zero releases".

Double the release cadence to achieve 9 months between major versions
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

This was originally proposed in PEP 596 and rejected as both too
irregular and too short.  One consequence of a 9 month release cadence
was shortening of the beta phase and this was considered dangerous.

Slow down releases but don't freeze feature development with Beta 1
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

This is described in PEP 598.  This proposal includes non-standard
concepts like the "incremental feature release" which makes it hard
to understand.  The presented advantages are unclear while the
unfamiliarity of the scheme poses a real risk of user and integrator
confusion.


Copyright
=========

This document is placed in the public domain or under the
CC0-1.0-Universal license, whichever is more permissive.

The [evidence index](evidence/index.txt) records revisions and SHA-256 hashes for two snapshots of PEP 602, *Annual Release Cycle for Python*, authored by Łukasz Langa, created 2019-06-04, type **Informational**, targeting Python 3.9: - [2019-09-10 draft](evidence/releases-2019-09-10.rst): historical proposal. - [2019-11-07 accepted text](evidence/releases-2019-11-07.rst): controlling policy in this packet; its header names Brett Cannon as BDFL-Delegate on behalf of the Steering Council. This establishes acceptance by the cutoff, not its exact date. Acceptance supersedes the draft rules identified below. It does not establish actual release dates, downstream adoption, runtime behavior or feature-specific exception approvals. No such evidence is supplied. Other PEPs are known here only through PEP 602's descriptions; their own texts are absent. Read [timing](#accepted-release-and-support-timing), [changes](#superseded-draft-decisions), [rationale](#rationale-and-rejected-alternatives), [governance](#dependent-governance-and-exceptions), then [unresolved evidence](#contradictions-and-verification-limits). ## Accepted release and support timing Authority: **Abstract**, **Implementation**, and **Example** in the [accepted snapshot](evidence/releases-2019-11-07.rst). | Area | Accepted rule at the cutoff | | --- | --- | | Release interval | Python 3.X.0 releases every 12 months, in October, starting with 3.9. The source calls these “major” versions. | | Development overlap | Development of 3.(X+1).0 starts at 3.X.0 Beta 1. The first five months overlap the preceding version's beta/RC stages and are unversioned. | | Alpha | Seven months of versioned alphas, accepting new features and bug fixes. | | Beta | Three months with four versioned betas; no new features, bug fixes allowed. | | Release candidate | Final two months with two RCs, or more if necessary, ending in the final release. | | Full support | First 18 months: bugfix updates and full releases (sources and Windows/macOS installers), approximately every other month. | | Security support | Next 42 months: security updates, with source-only releases as needed and no fixed cadence. | | End of support | Final source-only release five years after 3.X.0. | The text specifies around **17 months** of development (5 + 7 + 3 + 2). Its recurring calendar places finals after the annual core sprint and beta starts in late May after PyCon US sprints. The illustrative 3.9 schedule begins development on 2019-06-04, has seven alphas from 2019-10-14 through 2020-04-13, and freezes features at Beta 1 on 2020-05-18. Later betas are June 8, June 29 and July 20; RCs are August 10 and September 14; final is October 5, 2020. These are scheduled examples, not observed releases; [timing tensions remain](#contradictions-and-verification-limits). ## Superseded draft decisions Comparison sources: **Implementation**, **Example**, and **Risks** in the [September draft](evidence/releases-2019-09-10.rst), and **Implementation**, **Dependent Policies**, **Non-risks**, and **Rejected Ideas** in the [November accepted text](evidence/releases-2019-11-07.rst). | Earlier position (historical only) | Replacement and reason or limit | | --- | --- | | Four months of betas, one final RC month; one RC or more if needed. | Three beta months and two RC months, with two RCs or more. The cleaner old calendar was rejected to help Fedora integrate Python while both projects were developing, enabling early regression discovery and timely distribution. | | Example betas 2–4 on 2020-06-15, 07-13 and 08-17; RC 1 on 09-14, optional RC 2 on 09-21. | Replaced by the accepted example above. Development start, alpha dates, Beta 1 and final date remain unchanged. | | One year of roughly monthly bugfix releases, ending with 3.X.12 after the next feature release; four years of security-only support. | 18 months of bugfix/full releases about every other month, then 42 months security-only. The final 3.X.12 rule is removed; do not retain it as a requirement. Five-year total support remains. The accepted text says neither documented bugfix nor security support is shortened; it does not explicitly explain every support-text revision. | | Shorter bugfix support limited core maintenance cost but inconvenienced users; every n-th release as Python-2.7-style LTS was open for debate. | This draft tradeoff and open LTS option are superseded. The accepted text rejects extended Python-2.7-style support: every release already receives five years, including 18 months of regular bug fixes. No n or special LTS terms were approved. | | Deprecations, `__future__` defaults, Council and Release Manager terms all needed updates, without replacement rules. | Explicit retained release-count rules and an extension approval path now appear in Dependent Policies; see governance below. Other implicit dependencies remain possible. | | “Seventeen months” heading but “around 16 months” opening sentence; phases totaled 17 (5 + 7 + 4 + 1). | Opening sentence corrected to 17; revised phases still total 17. The example's elapsed duration remains a separate unresolved tension. | The accepted annual policy replaces the described 18-month release baseline at the upstream policy level. The older cadence remains useful historical context, not an operative instruction. Neither snapshot demonstrates downstream migration. ## Rationale and rejected alternatives Authority: **Rationale and Goals**, **Non-goals**, **Non-risks**, **Risks**, and **Rejected Ideas** in the [accepted snapshot](evidence/releases-2019-11-07.rst). Annual releases deliver smaller changes sooner, reduce upgrade difficulty and pressure to rush before Beta 1, and make contributor scheduling predictable. A longer explicit alpha phase offers meaningful progress snapshots; a shorter implicit “alpha 0” reduces overlap with the preceding unreleased version's beta. Alignment with distributors such as Fedora helps find core and third-party regressions early and supports community readiness from Day 1. The policy assumes neither more development resources nor faster feature growth or incompatibility. Users need not upgrade every release: every second release is offered as an experience similar to the preceding cadence. The accepted text says documented bugfix and security support are not shortened. Integrators still need to change their practices, and supporting all active versions eventually adds one or two versions to library/application testing matrices. | Alternative | Rejection and rationale recorded in PEP 602 | | --- | --- | | Keep the 18-month cadence | Irregular dates impede contributor planning. Rushed commits before and even after Beta 1 alternate with a false sense of spare time; rare workflow steps remain undocumented or unautomated. Larger releases raise upgrade costs, delay features and incompatible fixes for over a year, and make point-zero releases riskier for users who skip prerelease testing. | | Nine-month cadence | Originally proposed in PEP 596; too irregular and too short to gain annual-calendar benefits. Shortening development, especially beta/RC phases, was considered dangerous. | | Slower releases without a Beta 1 feature freeze | PEP 598's unfamiliar “incremental feature release” concepts were hard to understand, had unclear benefits, and risked user/integrator confusion. | The accepted **Example** also retains a counterfactual “if this PEP is rejected” 18-month schedule: alpha 1 on 2020-08-03, Beta 1 on 2020-11-30, final on 2021-04-19. Its “10 months later” alpha and “6 months later” beta/final annotations illustrate the cost of the old calendar; they are approximate comparisons, not an alternate active schedule. The old beta/RC split and extended LTS are rejected as recorded in [draft supersession](#superseded-draft-decisions). **Versioning is a non-goal.** Python 3.20 for October 2020 and 3.23 for October 2023 illustrate possible calendar names, not selected names. PEP 602 advocates neither for nor against renumbering; this would require a separate PEP. Acceptance of the annual calendar does not approve calendar versioning. ## Dependent governance and exceptions Authority: **Dependent Policies**, **Risks**, and **Rejected Ideas** in the [accepted snapshot](evidence/releases-2019-11-07.rst). - **Deprecations and `__future__`:** retain at least two releases before removing a deprecated feature or enabling a `__future__` behavior by default, described as the PEP 387 policy. “At least” is a minimum, not automatic removal on release two; do not substitute a newly inferred elapsed-time rule. - **Steering Council:** retain PEP 13's election after each feature release, yielding a consistent election schedule. - **Release Manager:** retain the previously undocumented two-feature-release convention. Extension to more releases requires approval from the Steering Council **and** the Cabal of Release Managers. The active Release Manager/PEP author offers to handle a third release to compensate for a shorter term; willingness is not evidence of extension approval. - **Scheduling allowance:** additional RCs are permitted if necessary. This does not waive the Beta 1 feature freeze; no feature-specific waiver is supplied. - **Support:** no extended Python-2.7-style support is planned. Historical discretionary bugfix overlap described below is not a new exception approval. The identified policies are addressed by the accepted PEP, superseding the draft's unspecified update list. Other policies may implicitly depend on release timing; the text explicitly leaves that risk open. Changes to the referenced PEPs or actual governance practice cannot be verified from this packet. ## Contradictions and verification limits - **Development duration:** September's heading/sentence conflict is corrected in November, whose heading, sentence and phase sum all say 17 months. However, both examples run from June 4, 2019 to October 5, 2020, roughly 16 months. Their initial unversioned interval also runs only to October 14, roughly four months rather than the stated five. The source does not reconcile nominal phase lengths with the example; preserve both pending authoritative clarification. - **Calendar precision:** both rationales say beta starts in “late May,” while both examples specify May 18. No exact recurring rule resolves that tension. - **Support documentation versus reported practice:** November's **Risks / The testing matrix** says PEP 101 allows only one last bugfix release after the next feature release, but at least the last four Python 3 versions reportedly overlapped the next stable version by around six months. It calls discretionary extended bugfix support uncodified and uses this practice to explain why stable overlap is not new. This is PEP 602's report of a documentation/practice mismatch, not independently checked release history or authority to infer extra support. - **Residual conditional wording:** despite its Accepted header, November retains “proposes,” an “if rejected” example and conditional adoption wording in Non-goals. Read those with the recorded acceptance status; they do not reopen the rejected schedule or authorize a versioning change. - **Missing figures and sources:** both snapshots reference release-calendar and support-matrix PNGs absent from the packet. November describes what its matrix includes, but the figures cannot be independently checked. Referenced PEPs and linked discussions are not supplied; local prose is the evidence boundary. Future updates should replace affected canonical statements in place, cite newly supplied authoritative evidence, and retain significant rationale and explicit supersession. Later policy, actual releases, downstream adoption and exception approvals each need their own evidence; none follows merely from acceptance.

PEP: 602
Title: Annual Release Cycle for Python
Version: $Revision$
Last-Modified: $Date$
Author: Łukasz Langa <lukasz@python.org>
Discussions-To: https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-602-annual-release-cycle-for-python/2296/
Status: Draft
Type: Informational
Content-Type: text/x-rst
Created: 04-Jun-2019
Python-Version: 3.9


Abstract
========

This document describes a change in the release calendar for Python
starting with Python 3.9.  This change accelerates the release cadence
such that major versions are released every twelve months.


Implementation
==============

Seventeen months to develop a major version
-------------------------------------------

This PEP proposes that Python 3.X.0 will be developed for around
16 months:

- The first *five months* overlap with Python 3.(X-1).0's beta
  and release candidate stages and are thus unversioned.

- The next *seven months* are spent on versioned alpha releases where
  both new features are incrementally added and bug fixes are included.

- The following *four months* are spent on versioned beta releases where
  **no new features** can be added but bug fixes are still included.

- The *final month* is spent on a release candidate (or more, if
  necessary) and concludes with the release of the final release of
  Python 3.X.0.

One year of full support, four more years of security fixes
-----------------------------------------------------------

After the relase of Python 3.X.0, the 3.X series is maintained for
five years:

- During the *first year* it receives bugfix updates approximately
  every month.  After the release of 3.(X+1).0 final, a final 3.X.12 is
  released.

- For the next *four years* it receives security updates and
  source-only releases are made on an as-needed basis
  (no monthly cadence).

- The final source-only release is made *five years* after 3.X.0.

Annual release cadence
----------------------

Feature development of Python 3.(X+1).0 starts as soon as
Python 3.X.0 Beta 1 is released.  This creates a twelve month delta
between major Python versions.


Example
=======

- 3.9 development begins: Tuesday, 2019-06-04
- 3.9.0 alpha 1: Monday, 2019-10-14
- 3.9.0 alpha 2: Monday, 2019-11-18
- 3.9.0 alpha 3: Monday, 2019-12-16
- 3.9.0 alpha 4: Monday, 2020-01-13
- 3.9.0 alpha 5: Monday, 2020-02-17
- 3.9.0 alpha 6: Monday, 2020-03-16
- 3.9.0 alpha 7: Monday, 2020-04-13
- 3.9.0 beta 1: Monday, 2020-05-18
  (No new features beyond this point.)

- 3.9.0 beta 2: Monday, 2020-06-15
- 3.9.0 beta 3: Monday, 2020-07-13
- 3.9.0 beta 4: Monday, 2020-08-17
- 3.9.0 candidate 1: Monday, 2020-09-14
- 3.9.0 candidate 2: Monday, 2020-09-21 (if necessary)
- 3.9.0 final: Monday, 2020-10-05

.. figure:: pep-0602-example-release-calendar.png
   :align: center
   :width: 100%

   Figure 1. Consequences of the annual release cycle on the calendar.


Rationale and Goals
===================

This change provides the following advantages:

- makes releases smaller: since doubling the cadence doesn't double our
  available development resources, consecutive releases are going to be
  smaller in terms of features;

- puts features and bug fixes in hands of users sooner;

- creates a more gradual upgrade path for users, by decreasing the
  surface of change in any single release;

- creates a predictable calendar for releases where the final release is
  always in October (so after the annual core sprint), and the beta
  phase starts in late May (so after PyCon US sprints);

- decreases the urge to rush features shortly before "Beta 1" due to
  the risk of them "slipping for 18 months";

- increases the explicit alpha release phase, which provides meaningful
  snapshots of progress on new features;

- significantly cuts the implicit "alpha 0" release phase which provides
  limited use for new development anyway (it overlaps with the beta of
  the *currently developed*, still unreleased, version);

Non-goals
---------

Adopting an annual release calendar allows for natural switching to
calendar versioning, for example by calling Python 3.9 "Python 3.20"
since it's released in October '20 and so on ("Python 3.23" would be the
one released in October '23).

While the ease of switching to calendar versioning can be treated as
an advantage of an annual release cycle, this PEP does not advocate for
or against a change in how Python is versioned.  Should the annual
release cycle be adopted, the versioning question will be dealt with in
a separate PEP.

Non-risks
---------

This change does not shorten the security updates calendar for a Python
release.

This change does not accelerate the velocity of development.  Python is
not going to become incompatible faster or accrue new features faster.
It's just that features are going to be released more gradually as they
are developed.

Consequently, while this change introduces the ability for users to
upgrade much faster, it does not require them to do so.  Say, if they
upgrade every second release, their experience with Python is going to
be very similar to the current situation.

Risks
-----

This requires changes to how integrators, like Linux distributions,
release Python within their systems.

This eventually increases the testing matrix for library and application
maintainers that want to support all actively supported Python versions
by one or two:

.. figure:: pep-0602-overlapping-support-matrix.png
   :align: center
   :width: 100%

   Figure 2. Testing matrix in the 18-month cadence vs. the 12-month

The following policies depend on the release cadence and will have to
be updated:

- the deprecation policy
- the``__future__`` import becoming the default
- the term of the Steering Council
- the term of the Release Manager

Finally, this shortens the bugfix period to twelve months.  This allows
core developers to increase the cadence without increasing the biggest
maintenance cost, however provides an inconvenience to the user.  This
particular risk might be solved by making every n-th release a LTS, in
the vein of Python 2.7.  This is open for debate.

Rejected Ideas
--------------

Keep the current 18 month release cadence
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

This is undesirable both for core developers and end users. From the
perspective of the core developer:

- it creates a surge of rushed commits before (and even after!) Beta 1
  due to the stress involved with "missing a release";

- ironically, after Beta 1 it creates a false sense of having "plenty of
  time" before the next release, time that passes quickly regardless;

- it causes certain elements of the workflow to be executed so rarely
  that they are not explicitly documented, let alone automated.

More importantly, from the perspective of the user:

- it creates releases with many new features, some being explicitly
  incompatible and some being accidentally incompatible, which makes
  the upgrade cost relatively high every time;

- it sits on features and incompatible bug fixes for over a year before
  becoming available to the user; and more specifically

- it causes every "point zero" release to be extra risky for users.
  While we provide and recommend testing with alphas and betas,
  "point zero" is the first release of a given Python version for many
  users.  The bigger a release is feature-wise, the more potential
  problems are hiding in "point zero releases".

Double the release cadence to achieve 9 months between major versions
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

This was originally proposed in PEP 596 and rejected as both too
irregular and too short.  One consequence of a 9 month release cadence
was shortening of the beta phase and this was considered dangerous.

Slow down releases but don't freeze feature development with Beta 1
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

This is described in PEP 598.  This proposal includes non-standard
concepts like the "incremental feature release" which makes it hard
to understand.  The presented advantages are unclear while the
unfamiliarity of the scheme poses a real risk of user and integrator
confusion.


Copyright
=========

This document is placed in the public domain or under the
CC0-1.0-Universal license, whichever is more permissive.

PEP: 602
Title: Annual Release Cycle for Python
Version: $Revision$
Last-Modified: $Date$
Author: Łukasz Langa <lukasz@python.org>
BDFL-Delegate: Brett Cannon (on behalf of the steering council)
Discussions-To: https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-602-annual-release-cycle-for-python/2296/
Status: Accepted
Type: Informational
Content-Type: text/x-rst
Created: 04-Jun-2019
Python-Version: 3.9


Abstract
========

This document describes a change in the release calendar for Python
starting with Python 3.9.  This change accelerates the release cadence
such that major versions are released predictably every twelve months,
in October every year.


Implementation
==============

Seventeen months to develop a major version
-------------------------------------------

This PEP proposes that Python 3.X.0 will be developed for around
17 months:

- The first *five months* overlap with Python 3.(X-1).0's beta
  and release candidate stages and are thus unversioned.

- The next *seven months* are spent on versioned alpha releases where
  both new features are incrementally added and bug fixes are included.

- The following *three months* are spent on four versioned beta releases
  where **no new features** can be added but bug fixes are still
  included.

- The final *two months* are spent on two release candidates (or more,
  if necessary) and conclude with the release of the final release of
  Python 3.X.0.

1½ year of full support, 3½ more years of security fixes
--------------------------------------------------------

After the release of Python 3.X.0, the 3.X series is maintained for
five years:

- During the *first eighteen months* (1½ year) it receives bugfix
  updates and full releases (sources and installers for Windows and
  macOS) are made approximately every other month.

- For the next *forty two months* (3½ years) it receives security
  updates and source-only releases are made on an as-needed basis
  (no fixed cadence).

- The final source-only release is made *five years* after 3.X.0.

Annual release cadence
----------------------

Feature development of Python 3.(X+1).0 starts as soon as
Python 3.X.0 Beta 1 is released.  This creates a twelve month delta
between major Python versions.


Example
=======

- 3.9 development begins: Tuesday, 2019-06-04
- 3.9.0 alpha 1: Monday, 2019-10-14
- 3.9.0 alpha 2: Monday, 2019-11-18
- 3.9.0 alpha 3: Monday, 2019-12-16
- 3.9.0 alpha 4: Monday, 2020-01-13
- 3.9.0 alpha 5: Monday, 2020-02-17
- 3.9.0 alpha 6: Monday, 2020-03-16
- 3.9.0 alpha 7: Monday, 2020-04-13
- 3.9.0 beta 1: Monday, 2020-05-18
  (No new features beyond this point.)

- 3.9.0 beta 2: Monday, 2020-06-08
- 3.9.0 beta 3: Monday, 2020-06-29
- 3.9.0 beta 4: Monday, 2020-07-20
- 3.9.0 candidate 1: Monday, 2020-08-10
- 3.9.0 candidate 2: Monday, 2020-09-14
- 3.9.0 final: Monday, 2020-10-05

.. figure:: pep-0602-example-release-calendar.png
   :align: center
   :width: 100%

   Figure 1. Consequences of the annual release cycle on the calendar.

In comparison, if this PEP is rejected and Python keeps the current
release schedule:

- 3.9 development begins: Tuesday, 2019-06-04
- 3.9.0 alpha 1: Monday, 2020-08-03  (10 months later)
- 3.9.0 alpha 2: Monday, 2020-09-07
- 3.9.0 alpha 3: Monday, 2020-10-05
- 3.9.0 alpha 4: Monday, 2020-11-02
- 3.9.0 beta 1: Monday, 2020-11-30  (6 months later)
- 3.9.0 beta 2: Monday, 2021-01-04
- 3.9.0 beta 3: Monday, 2021-02-01
- 3.9.0 beta 4: Monday, 2021-03-01
- 3.9.0 candidate 1: Monday, 2021-03-29
- 3.9.0 candidate 2: Monday, 2021-04-05 (if necessary)
- 3.9.0 final: Monday, 2021-04-19  (6 months later)


Dependent Policies
==================

Deprecations
------------

The current policy around breaking changes assumes at least two releases
before a deprecated feature is removed from Python or a ``__future__``
behavior is enabled by default.  This is documented in PEP 387.

This PEP proposes to keep this policy of **at least** two releases
before making a breaking change.

The term of the Steering Council
--------------------------------

The current wording of PEP 13 states that "a new council is elected
after each feature release".  This PEP proposes to keep this policy
as it will lead to a consistent election schedule.

The term of the Release Manager
-------------------------------

The current undocumented convention is for a single Release Manager to
handle two feature releases of Python.  This PEP proposes to keep this
policy, allowing for the term to be extended to more releases with
approval from the Steering Council and the Cabal of Release Managers.

In particular, since this PEP is authored by the active Release Manager
and its effect would shorten the term of the Release Manager, the author
is open to managing the release of a third feature release to compensate
for the disruption.


Rationale and Goals
===================

This change provides the following advantages:

- makes releases smaller: since doubling the cadence doesn't double our
  available development resources, consecutive releases are going to be
  smaller in terms of features;

- puts features and bug fixes in hands of users sooner;

- creates a more gradual upgrade path for users, by decreasing the
  surface of change in any single release;

- creates a predictable calendar for releases where the final release is
  always in October (so after the annual core sprint), and the beta
  phase starts in late May (so after PyCon US sprints), which is
  especially important for core developers who need to plan to include
  Python involvement in their calendar;

- decreases the urge to rush features shortly before "Beta 1" due to
  the risk of them "slipping for 18 months";

- allows for synchronizing the schedule of Python release management
  with external distributors like Fedora who've been historically very
  helpful in finding regressions early not only in core Python but also
  in third-party libraries, helping moving the community forward to
  support the latest version of Python from Day 1;

- increases the explicit alpha release phase, which provides meaningful
  snapshots of progress on new features;

- significantly cuts the implicit "alpha 0" release phase which provides
  limited use for new development anyway (it overlaps with the beta of
  the *currently developed*, still unreleased, version).

Non-goals
---------

Adopting an annual release calendar allows for natural switching to
calendar versioning, for example by calling Python 3.9 "Python 3.20"
since it's released in October '20 and so on ("Python 3.23" would be the
one released in October '23).

While the ease of switching to calendar versioning can be treated as
an advantage of an annual release cycle, this PEP does not advocate for
or against a change in how Python is versioned.  Should the annual
release cycle be adopted, the versioning question will be dealt with in
a separate PEP.

Non-risks
---------

This change does not shorten the currently documented support calendar
for a Python release, both in terms of bugfix releases and security
fixes.

This change does not accelerate the velocity of development.  Python is
not going to become incompatible faster or accrue new features faster.
It's just that features are going to be released more gradually as they
are developed.

Consequently, while this change introduces the ability for users to
upgrade much faster, it does not require them to do so.  Say, if they
upgrade every second release, their experience with Python is going to
be similar to the current situation.

Risks
-----

Python redistribution
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

This requires changes to how integrators, like Linux distributions,
release Python within their systems.

The testing matrix
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

This eventually increases the testing matrix for library and application
maintainers that want to support all actively supported Python versions
by one or two:

.. figure:: pep-0602-overlapping-support-matrix.png
   :align: center
   :width: 50%

   Figure 2. Testing matrix in the 18-month cadence vs. the 12-month

The "extended bugfix support at the discretion of the Release Manager"
stage of the current release cycle is not codified.  If fact, PEP 101
currently states that after the release of Python 3.(X+1).0 only one
last bugfix release is made for Python 3.X.0.  However, in practice at
least the last four versions of Python 3 overlapped with stable releases
of the next version for around six months.  Figure 2 is including
this information to demonstrate that overlap between stable version
releases with the 12-month release cadence will be nothing new.

Other policies may depend on the release cadence
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Although identified dependent policies were addressed in a previous
section, it is entirely possible there are some other areas which
implicitly rely on the timing of Python releases.


Rejected Ideas
--------------

Keep the current 18 month release cadence
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

This is undesirable both for core developers and end users. From the
perspective of the core developer:

- it makes contribution scheduling harder due to irregular release
  dates every year;

- it creates a surge of rushed commits before (and even after!) Beta 1
  due to the stress involved with "missing a release";

- ironically, after Beta 1 it creates a false sense of having "plenty of
  time" before the next release, time that passes quickly regardless;

- it causes certain elements of the workflow to be executed so rarely
  that they are not explicitly documented, let alone automated.

More importantly, from the perspective of the user:

- it creates releases with many new features, some being explicitly
  incompatible and some being accidentally incompatible, which makes
  the upgrade cost relatively high every time;

- it sits on features and incompatible bug fixes for over a year before
  becoming available to the user; and more specifically

- it causes every "point zero" release to be extra risky for users.
  While we provide and recommend testing with alphas and betas,
  "point zero" is the first release of a given Python version for many
  users.  The bigger a release is feature-wise, the more potential
  problems are hiding in "point zero releases".

Double the release cadence to achieve 9 months between major versions
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

This was originally proposed in PEP 596 and rejected as both too
irregular and too short.  This would not give any of the benefits of
a regular release calendar but it would shorten all development phases,
especially the beta + RC phases.  This was considered dangerous.

Keep "4 betas over 4 months and a final month for the release candidate"
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

While this would make the release calendar a bit cleaner, `it would make
it very hard for external distributors like Fedora
<https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-602-annual-release-cycle-for-python/2296/79?u=ambv>`_
to release the newest version of Python as soon as possible.  We are
adjusting Python's calendar here in the hope that this will enable
Fedora to integrate the newest version of Python with the newest version
of Fedora *as both are being developed* which makes both projects
better.

Slow down releases but don't freeze feature development with Beta 1
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

This is described in PEP 598.  This proposal includes non-standard
concepts like the "incremental feature release" which makes it hard
to understand.  The presented advantages are unclear while the
unfamiliarity of the scheme poses a real risk of user and integrator
confusion.

Long-Term Support Releases
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Each version of Python is effectively long-term support: it's supported
for five years, with the first eighteen months allowing regular bug
fixes and security updates.  For the remaining time security updates are
accepted and promptly released.

No extended support in the vein of Python 2.7 is planned going forward.
